title: Statistics Reference
text: A lookup sheet, not a tutorial. Each term has a plain-English meaning, a Tidebreak example and the mistake people make with it. Every number on this page is computed from the playtest data when the site is built. The notes teach these ideas; this page is for checking one quickly during a lab.

title: Statistics Reference
text:
Describing data
Taught in Planning a Playtest and Data, Variables and Types.



Term
What it means
Tidebreak example
The common mistake




Observation
One unit you measured. Read it as: one row.
One player in one session: 120 observations in tidebreak_sessions.csv.
Mixing units in one table, such as session rows and per-player totals side by side.


Variable
One thing recorded about every observation. Read it as: one column.
session_minutes, cohort, deaths: 26 variables in all.
Spreading one variable across several columns, as a survey export does with its questions.


Categorical
Values are labels. Nominal labels have no order; ordinal labels do, with unknown gaps.
quit_reason is nominal, with 4 categories. cohort is ordinal: Novice, Regular, Veteran.
Averaging a category because it was coded as 1, 2, 3.


Numerical
Values are quantities, so arithmetic on them means something.
score, deaths, session_minutes.
Treating an ID or a 1–5 rating as a plain number without thinking about it.


Discrete
Numerical values that are counts: whole numbers only.
deaths runs from 0 to 7.
Drawing a histogram with more bars than there are possible values, which leaves gaps that look like a pattern.


Continuous
Numerical values that can fall anywhere in a range.
session_minutes, frames$ms.
Tabulating it with table(); almost every value is unique. Use a histogram.


Sample
The observations you actually have.
120 sessions from 30 players.
Forgetting to report how many (rule 8).


Population
Everyone the conclusion is meant to apply to. You never measure it.
Everyone who will play Tidebreak after launch.
Assuming the sample looks like the population. A studio’s Discord is not its audience.

title: Statistics Reference
text:
Centre and spread
Taught in Describing Variables.









Term
What it means
Tidebreak example
The common mistake




Mean
The total divided by the count. Read it as: the value if everyone were equal.
Mean session length 22.8 minutes.
Quoting it for skewed data, where a few extreme values drag it away from most players.


Median
The middle value when sorted. Half above, half below.
Median session length 26.1 minutes.
Assuming it is always better. It ignores how extreme the extremes are, which is sometimes the point.


Mode
The most common value. The only centre a nominal variable has.
The most common number of deaths in a session is 4; the median is 3.
Treating it as a substitute for the median on a continuous variable, where almost every value is unique.


Minimum / maximum
The smallest and largest values.
Session length from 7.7 to 32 minutes.
Skipping them. They are the fastest way to spot an impossible value.


Range
Maximum minus minimum.
24.3 minutes for session length.
Using it as the measure of spread. One unusual player sets it.


Standard deviation
The typical distance of a value from the mean.
Frame time: 1.05 ms in Build A, 3.40 ms in Build B.
Quoting it for skewed data. It inherits every weakness of the mean.


Variance
The average squared distance from the mean; the SD squared.
Session length: 60.3 square minutes.
Reporting it. Its units are squared, so the SD, its square root, is the one to quote.


Interquartile range (IQR)
The width of the middle half of the data.
13.8 minutes for session length.
Forgetting it exists. For skewed data, quote the median and IQR together.


Percentile
The value with that percentage of the data below it.
99th percentile frame time: 19.5 ms in Build A, 39.4 ms in Build B.
Stopping at the 95th, which cannot see a problem rarer than one case in twenty.

title: Statistics Reference
text:
Shape
Taught in Distributions and Shape.



Term
What it means
Tidebreak example
The common mistake




Distribution
The full pattern of values: which occur and how often. A histogram draws it.
Sentinel score has two humps: games that anchor the round and games that collapse early.
Summarising a two-humped distribution with one average, which describes neither group (rule 4).


Skew
A distribution with a long tail on one side. The mean is pulled towards the tail.
Session length is left-skewed: mean 22.8 below median 26.1, pulled down by early quits.
Reading the gap between mean and median without comparing it to the size of the variable.


Bimodal
A distribution with two humps, usually two groups mixed together.
Build A session length: one group quits around minutes 10 to 14, another plays to the end.
Describing it with one average or one boxplot, neither of which can show two humps.


Normal distribution
The symmetric bell curve, defined by its mean and SD. About 68% of values lie within 1 SD of the mean and 95% within 2.
Awareness is close to normal: 65% of sessions within 1 SD. Session length is not: 57%.
Assuming it. Most game measures are bounded and skewed; check by laying the curve over the histogram.


z-score
How many SDs a value sits from the mean.
An awareness rating of 90 has z = 1.9.
Reading it with the 68–95–99.7 rule when the data is not roughly normal.


Retention curve
The share of sessions still going at each point in time.
Build A: 88% still playing at minute 11, 68% at minute 13.
Summarising “how long players stayed” with a mean, which hides when they left.


Outlier
A value far from the rest. A boxplot draws each one as a point.
The boxplot of score flags 7 low values, all of them Sentinel games.
Deleting it. An outlier is an error, an extreme player or the finding; find out which first (rule 6).

title: Statistics Reference
text:
From sample to population
Taught in From Sample to Population.









Term
What it means
Tidebreak example
The common mistake




Sampling variability
A different sample gives different numbers, even from the same population.
Split the sessions into four batches of 30 in file order: mean scores 1550, 1313, 1462, 1390.
Treating one playtest’s numbers as fixed facts about the game.


Sampling distribution
The distribution of a summary, such as a mean, across every sample you might have drawn.
1,000 simulated playtests of 30 give 1,000 different mean session lengths, forming a bell.
Confusing it with the distribution of the players. It is the distribution of the estimate.


Standard error
The SD of the sampling distribution: how far an estimate is typically off. SE = SD / √n.
Build B mean session length: SE 0.9 minutes, from an SD of 6.94 and n = 60.
Reporting it as the spread of the players. The SD describes players; the SE describes the estimate.


Central limit theorem
Means of reasonably large samples are approximately normal, whatever the shape of the data.
Session length is skewed and two-humped, but means of 30 sessions form a bell.
Assuming it rescues tiny samples, or summaries other than the mean such as the 99th percentile.


Confidence interval
A range of plausible values for the population, given the sample. Wider means less certain.
Build B sessions ran between 0.2 and 5.7 minutes longer than Build A (95% interval).
Reading “95%” as the chance this particular interval is right. It describes how often the method captures the true value.

title: Statistics Reference
text:
Testing a difference
Taught in Comparing Groups.









Term
What it means
Tidebreak example
The common mistake




Null hypothesis
The claim that there is no difference, which the test tries to find evidence against.
Build A and Build B have the same mean session length.
Believing the test can prove it. Failing to find a difference is not showing there is none.


Alternative hypothesis
The claim that there is a difference.
Mean session length differs between the builds.
Choosing a one-sided direction after seeing which way the data went.


Permutation test
Shuffle the group labels many times to see what differences chance alone produces; the p-value is the share of shuffles at least as extreme as the real result.
Wrong turns: the real gap is 3.4; the largest of 2,000 shuffles is 1.97.
Forgetting it works for any summary, including a median or a 99th percentile.


p-value
How surprising the data would be if the null hypothesis were true. Small means surprising.
Session length by build: p = 0.037.
Reading it as the probability that the null hypothesis is true. It is not.


Significance level (α)
The p-value threshold, chosen before looking, usually 0.05. It is also the false-alarm rate.
A 0.05 threshold flags about 1 in 20 comparisons of builds that do not really differ.
Choosing it after seeing the p-value.


Type I error
A false alarm: concluding there is a difference when there is none.
Rebuilding a level because of a fluke result.
Ignoring that it becomes likely when many tests are run.


Type II error
A missed effect: finding no significant difference when there is one.
Shipping a problem because the playtest was too small to see it.
Reading “not significant” as “no difference”.


Power
The chance a test detects a real effect of a given size. Grows with sample size.
Even Tidebreak’s large signposting effect is missed more often than not with five sessions per build.
Running a small playtest and concluding the change did nothing.


Statistical significance
A p-value below a threshold set in advance, conventionally 0.05.
Session length differs (p = 0.037); score does not (p = 0.822).
Treating “significant” as “important”. It means “unlikely to be chance alone”, nothing more.


Practical significance
Whether a difference is big enough to change a design decision.
In the Atrium, Build B’s frames are 0.42 ms faster (p < 0.001): highly significant and imperceptible to any player.
Reporting a tiny, significant difference as a win. Always give the size of the difference too.


Effect size
How big the difference is: in the original units with its interval, or standardised (Cohen’s d).
3.4 fewer wrong turns per session in Build B.
Reporting a p-value without it.


Two-proportion test
Compares two percentages, such as quit rates. prop.test(counts, totals)
Frustration quits: 20 of 60 in Build A against 5 of 60 in Build B, p = 0.002.
Using a t-test on a yes/no outcome, or comparing raw counts from groups of different sizes.


Multiple comparisons
Running many tests, which raises the chance that at least one is a false alarm.
Eight survey items tested at 0.05: a 34% chance of at least one false alarm if nothing differed.
Scanning every column and reporting what came up. Decide the comparisons in advance.


Independent-samples t-test
Compares two group means when different people are in each group. t.test(y ~ group)
t.test(session_minutes ~ build): every player saw only one build.
Ignoring that each player contributed 4 sessions, so the sessions are not fully independent of one another.


Paired t-test
Compares two measurements taken on the same people. t.test(x, y, paired = TRUE)
Not possible on the sessions file: 0 of 30 players played both builds. In tidebreak_paired.csv, 30 players played both and took 2.8 fewer wrong turns in Build B (p < 0.001).
Running a paired test on unpaired data, or an independent test when the same players did both.

title: Statistics Reference
text:
Relationships
Taught in Relationships and Correlation. Rows marked (Going further) are on Regression.









Term
What it means
Tidebreak example
The common mistake




Correlation
How closely two numerical variables move together, from −1 (opposite) through 0 (unrelated) to +1 (together).
Awareness and score: 0.59, the strongest of the ability ratings. Shots fired and score: 0.05. Mobility and survivability: -0.66, a trade-off.
Calling a correlation “strong” without context. Whether 0.3 matters depends on the question.


Spearman correlation
Correlation of the ranks: does one tend to go up when the other does? cor(x, y, method = "spearman")
Deaths and difficulty rating: 0.57 (Pearson gives 0.58).
Using Pearson on 1–7 ratings without checking that the two agree.


Correlation matrix
The correlation of every chosen measure with every other. d \|> select(...) \|> cor()
Deaths, wrong turns, difficulty, enjoyment and session length: deaths and difficulty go together most; wrong turns go with nothing.
Putting every column in. Choose the 3–5 measures that answer your question, and draw the pairs.


Confounding variable
A third variable that drives both of the variables you are comparing.
Veterans average 75.6 awareness against 57.3 for Novices, and a median score of 1664 against 1281. Experience could be driving both.
Reporting a relationship without asking what else differs between the players at each end of it.


Simpson’s paradox
A relationship that reverses when the data is split into groups.
Mobility and survivability: -0.66 overall, but positive within every archetype (0.3 to 0.6).
Drawing a conclusion about individuals from a trend that only exists between groups.


Simple linear regression (Going further)
The straight line that best predicts one variable from another. lm(y ~ x)
lm(score ~ awareness): predicted score = 426 + 15.2 × awareness.
Reading the slope as the effect of changing x, rather than how x and y move together.


Slope (Going further)
The average change in y for each one-unit increase in x.
15.2 points of score per point of awareness.
Quoting it without its confidence interval or units.


Residual (Going further)
Actual minus predicted: how far one observation sits from the line.
The largest negative residuals in the awareness regression are Sentinel collapses.
Ignoring them. The cases the line cannot explain are often the finding.


R² (Going further)
The share of the variation in y that the line accounts for; in simple regression, the correlation squared.
Awareness accounts for 35% of the variation in score.
Reading a low R² as “useless” or a high one as “causal”.


Extrapolation (Going further)
Using a line to predict outside the range of the data.
Awareness ratings run from 38 to 95; the line says nothing outside that range.
Interpreting the intercept when x = 0 is impossible.


Correlation versus causation
Two things moving together does not show that one causes the other.
Buffing awareness would not necessarily raise score; the players with high awareness may simply be better players.
Turning “is associated with” into “causes” between the analysis and the design meeting.

title: Statistics Reference
text:
Which tool for which question









The question
Look at
Summarise with
Test with




What was a typical session like?
Histogram
Median and IQR
—


How bad does the worst case get?
Histogram or trace
95th and 99th percentiles
—


Do two builds differ, with different players on each?
Side-by-side boxplots
Medians, IQRs, difference in means
Independent-samples t-test


Do two builds differ, with the same players on both?
Each player’s difference
Mean difference
Paired t-test


Do two numerical variables move together?
Scatterplot
Correlation: Pearson, or Spearman for ratings
—


Which of several measures go together?
pairs()
Correlation matrix of 3–5 measures
—


Does a relationship hold within groups?
Scatterplot coloured or faceted by group
Correlation per group with group_by()
—


Is a difference worth acting on?
The size of the difference and its confidence interval
—
No test answers this; it is a design judgement




See also: Ten Rules, R and Quarto Reference.

Describing one variable







Task
Code




Centre
mean(x), median(x)


Spread

Quartiles

A specific percentile
quantile(x, 0.99)

Count a category

Biggest first, with proportions

Code




Summaries per group

Cleaning







Task
Code




Which values are missing

Missing values in every column
colSums(is.na(d))


Rows with a blank in a column
d \|> filter(is.na(session_minutes))


Remove repeated rows
d <- d \|> distinct()


Keys that appear more than once
d \|> count(session_id) \|> filter(n > 1)


Strip spaces and fix case
d \|> mutate(cohort = tolower(trimws(cohort)))


Fix the order of categories
d \|> mutate(cohort = factor(cohort, levels = c("novice", "regular", "veteran")))

d \|> count(cohort), before and after


Text to numbers
as.numeric(x) (unreadable values become NA)


Does text contain a word

Are two objects exactly the same
identical(a, b)


The same jobs (recognise)

Record every row you drop, why, and the n before and after. Cleaning is analysis.

Transforming with dplyr
Load with library(dplyr). Each verb takes a data frame and returns one.







Task
Code




Pass a result into the next function
d \|> filter(build == "A")


Keep rows
d \|> filter(build == "A", score > 1500)


Keep rows matching either condition
d \|> filter(is.na(deaths) \| is.na(session_minutes))


Keep columns
d \|> select(session_id, build, score)


Add or change a column

One column as a vector, in a pipe

Width of an interval

title: Combining Evidence
Combining Evidence
text:
Why This Matters for Playtesting
By the end of a project your team has numbers from the game, notes from watching people play, survey ratings and a pile of comments. It is tempting to report the source that tells the best story. The reader cannot see what you left out.
The strongest findings use more than one source. “Players got lost less” from telemetry alone is a count. Add an observer who saw players stop backtracking at the junction, and players who wrote that the route was obvious, and it is a finding nobody will argue with.
The most interesting findings are where the sources disagree. Tidebreak has one. It is the worked example at the end of this page.

title: Combining Evidence
text:
Three Sources, Three Questions









Source
Answers
Strength
Weakness




Telemetry
What happened in the game?
Complete, precise, cheap at scale
Says nothing about why, or how it felt


Observation
How did the player’s behaviour unfold?
Sees hesitation, confusion and workarounds that leave no trace in a log
Slow; one observer sees one player; observers see what they expect


Self-report
What does the player say they experienced?
The only source for feelings, intentions and opinions
Players misremember, are polite, and do not notice everything



Choose measures from at least two sources for every question that matters. That decision is made when you plan the playtest, not when you write the report (Planning a Playtest).

Recording observation
Observation is only evidence if it is recorded the same way for every player. Write a short observation sheet before the playtest, with the behaviours you expect to matter, and tick or time-stamp them as they happen:









Time
Location
Behaviour
Note




02:10
First junction
Backtracked
Went left, returned


02:45
First junction
Hesitated > 5 s
Looked at the ceiling lights


06:30
Corridor
Asked a question
“Where am I meant to go?”



Fix the behaviour list in advance: backtracked, hesitated more than 5 seconds, asked for help, ignored a prompt. Then observations can be counted per player, exactly like telemetry, and joined to it on the player ID.
For your project: if your team watched playtests but did not write anything down, say so in the limitations. Next time, take an observation sheet with three to five behaviours on it.

title: Combining Evidence
text:
Coding Comments
Free text is the richest self-report you have, and the hardest to use. Coding turns it into something you can count: read the comments, decide on a small set of codes, and give each comment one.

Step 1: read everything first
Before writing a single code, read every comment. Tidebreak has 120 comments, but only 10 different sentences:

sessions |> count(comment, sort = TRUE)

# A tibble: 10 × 2
   comment                                     n
   <chr>                                   <int>
 1 Died a lot but it felt fair.               22
 2 Ran in circles for a while.                16
 3 Got lost after the first room.             15
 4 No idea what the objective was.            13
 5 Too hard for a first attempt.              13
 6 Could not tell where I was meant to go.    10
 7 Enjoyed it, would play again.              10
 8 Lighting made the exit easy to spot.       10
 9 The route was obvious this time.            6
10 The signposting helped.                     5


Real comments will be messier, longer and more varied. Read them anyway.


Step 2: write a codebook
A codebook lists each code, what counts as that code, and an example. Keep it to four to six codes; more than that and nobody can apply them consistently.








Code
Use when the comment…
Example




Lost or unclear
says the player did not know where to go or what to do
“Ran in circles for a while.”


Found the way
says navigation or guidance worked
“Lighting made the exit easy to spot.”


Difficulty
is about dying, challenge or fairness
“Too hard for a first attempt.”


General
is anything else
“Enjoyed it, would play again.”



The codebook goes in an appendix. A reader needs to see your codes to judge your counts, exactly as they need your cleaning log to judge your n.


Step 3: apply the codes in R
grepl() returns TRUE when a comment contains any of the words you give it, and case_when() gives each comment the first code that matches:

coded <- sessions |>
  mutate(code = case_when(
    grepl("lost|circles|meant to go|objective", comment) ~ "Lost or unclear",
    grepl("route|exit|signposting", comment)             ~ "Found the way",
    grepl("Died|hard", comment)                          ~ "Difficulty",
    TRUE                                                 ~ "General"
  ))

coded |> count(code)

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  code                n
  <chr>           <int>
1 Difficulty         35
2 Found the way      21
3 General            10
4 Lost or unclear    54


| inside the quotes means “or”. TRUE ~ "General" catches everything left over.


Step 4: check by hand
Keyword matching is fast and blunt. Read a sample of comments next to their codes, and fix the codebook or the keywords until they agree with what you would have decided:

coded |> distinct(comment, code)

# A tibble: 10 × 2
   comment                                 code           
   <chr>                                   <chr>          
 1 Could not tell where I was meant to go. Lost or unclear
 2 The signposting helped.                 Found the way  
 3 Lighting made the exit easy to spot.    Found the way  
 4 Got lost after the first room.          Lost or unclear
 5 Too hard for a first attempt.           Difficulty     
 6 Died a lot but it felt fair.            Difficulty     
 7 Ran in circles for a while.             Lost or unclear
 8 The route was obvious this time.        Found the way  
 9 No idea what the objective was.         Lost or unclear
10 Enjoyed it, would play again.           General        


With real comments, check at least twenty. If two people on the team code the same twenty comments separately and disagree often, the codebook is not clear enough yet.


Step 5: count by group, then read what you counted

coded |> count(code, build)

# A tibble: 8 × 3
  code            build     n
  <chr>           <chr> <int>
1 Difficulty      A        19
2 Difficulty      B        16
3 Found the way   A        12
4 Found the way   B         9
5 General         A         6
6 General         B         4
7 Lost or unclear A        23
8 Lost or unclear B        31


Codes are counts of what players chose to write, not rates of what happened. Report them as “31 of 60 Build B comments mentioned being lost or unclear”, not as “52% of Build B players got lost”.


Quotes as evidence
Quote a comment to show a pattern, never to be the pattern. One vivid quote beside a chart of frustration quits makes the chart human. One vivid quote instead of the chart is an anecdote. Pick quotes that are typical of their code, say how many comments the code covers, and never quote only the comments that agree with you.

title: Combining Evidence
text:
Triangulation
Triangulation means checking a finding against more than one source. Three outcomes are possible, and each tells you something different:








The sources…
What it means
What to write




Agree
The finding is strong
Lead with it, and cite every source


Disagree
One source is measuring something different from what you thought
Report both, and explain which to trust for which question


Only one source has anything
The finding rests on one kind of evidence
Report it with that caveat, and plan the missing source for the next test









flowchart TD
  F["One finding"] --> T["Telemetry"]
  F --> O["Observation"]
  F --> S["Self-report"]
  T --> Q{"Do they agree?"}
  O --> Q
  S --> Q
  Q -->|Yes| A(["Strong finding"])
  Q -->|No| D(["Explain the gap"])
  class D accent




Figure 1: Agreement makes a finding strong. Disagreement is not a failure: it tells you what each source is really measuring.

title: Combining Evidence
text:
Worked Example
The telemetry says Build B fixed navigation. Do the players agree? Put every source on the navigation question side by side.
Telemetry. Build A players averaged 8.9 wrong turns per session; Build B players 5.5. Large, and very unlikely to be chance (Comparing Groups).
Self-report, ratings. “The level was easy to navigate” averaged 3.2 in Build A and 3.23 in Build B: no change. Across sessions it does not correlate with wrong turns at all (Spearman r = 0.05). “I always knew what my objective was” did improve, from 2.13 to 3.08.
Self-report, comments. 31 Build B comments were coded lost or unclear, against 23 in Build A: the opposite of the telemetry. And 3 Build A players wrote that “the signposting helped”, about the build without the new signage. Split by enjoyment instead of build, the codes separate cleanly:

coded |> count(code, enjoyed = enjoyment >= 5)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  code            enjoyed     n
  <chr>           <lgl>   <int>
1 Difficulty      FALSE      35
2 Found the way   TRUE       21
3 General         TRUE       10
4 Lost or unclear FALSE      54


Every found the way comment came from a player who rated enjoyment 5 or above, and every lost or unclear comment from one who rated it lower. The comments record how the session felt, not where the player went.
Observation. Tidebreak did not record any. That is the gap this example exposes.
Putting it together.

What happened: Build B cut wrong turns. Only telemetry measured it directly, and it is the source to trust for what happened.
What players noticed: not much. The navigation rating did not move, and players appear not to know when they are lost.
What the comments measure: mood. Useful for knowing how the session felt; weak evidence about navigation in either direction.
What is missing: someone watching the junctions, to see whether players hesitate and backtrack, and whether they seem aware of it.

What should the team do? Keep Build B’s guidance on the strength of the telemetry. Stop relying on the navigation rating to check navigation on this level. In the next playtest, add an observation sheet for the first two junctions, so the telemetry and the observation can be compared directly.
In the Discussion you would write: “The reduction in wrong turns was not reflected in players’ navigation ratings or comments. The comments tracked enjoyment rather than build, which suggests they describe how the session felt rather than where the player went. We treat the telemetry as the evidence for navigation, and recommend structured observation at the junctions in the next playtest to check whether players notice when they are lost.”

title: Combining Evidence
text:
Writing Limitations
Every playtest has weaknesses. Naming them is not an admission of failure: it is what lets the reader trust everything else. A limitation you name costs you less than one the reader finds.
A good limitation is specific to your playtest, says what it might change, and says whether you checked it.








Kind
Generic (weak)
Specific (useful)




Sample
“The sample was small.”
“30 players; how they were recruited was not recorded, so we cannot say how closely they match the game’s audience.”


Design
“There may be confounds.”
“Each player played one build, so differences between the two groups of players could explain part of the gap. The cohort mix in each build is in Appendix C.”


Independence
“Data may not be independent.”
“Each player contributed 4 sessions. The result holds when each player counts once.”


Measurement
“Surveys are subjective.”
“The navigation rating did not track wrong turns, so it is not a reliable check on navigation for this level.”


Coding
“Comments were interpreted.”
“Comments were coded by keyword into four codes (Appendix B); a second coder was not used.”


Not measured
“More research is needed.”
“No observation was recorded, so we cannot say whether players noticed when they were lost.”



Limitations go in the Discussion, close to the claims they qualify. The Conclusion should already take them into account.
For your project: write your limitations as you go, not on the last night. Each time you make a decision you are not sure about (a row dropped, a code merged, a measure you could not collect), add a line.

title: Combining Evidence
text:
Common Mistakes
Reporting only the source that tells the best story. The reader cannot see what you left out. Report every source you collected on the question.
Treating a count of comments as a rate. A comment is what a player chose to write. “Ten players mentioned the lighting” is not “ten players noticed the lighting”.
Coding without a codebook. If the reader cannot see what each code means, they cannot judge the counts.
Too many codes. Fifteen codes on sixty comments gives counts of two and three. Four to six is plenty.
One quote as the finding. A quote illustrates a pattern; it cannot be one.
Explaining away a disagreement. When telemetry and self-report disagree, the disagreement is a finding. Report it and say what each source is measuring.
Generic limitations. “The sample was small” tells the reader nothing they can use.

title: Combining Evidence
text:
Practice
Each takes two or three minutes.

Classify. Which source is each of these? (a) A death count. (b) “Player paused for 20 seconds at the bridge.” (c) A 1–7 enjoyment rating. (d) The time at which a player first opened the map. (e) “I didn’t know I could sprint.”
Compute. Among frustration quits only, which comment code is most common?
Critique. “12 of 60 players complained about the camera, so the camera is a problem for 20% of players.” What is wrong?
Rewrite. Make this limitation specific: “There may be other factors that affected the results.”







NoteShow answers





1. (a) Telemetry. (b) Observation. (c) Self-report. (d) Telemetry. (e) Self-report.
2.

coded |>
  filter(quit_reason == "Frustrated") |>
  count(code, sort = TRUE)

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  code                n
  <chr>           <int>
1 Difficulty         12
2 Lost or unclear     9
3 Found the way       2
4 General             2


Difficulty, with 12, ahead of lost or unclear with 9. Yet the survey says frustration quitters did not know their objective. Players name the symptom they felt, not the cause, which is why comments illustrate a finding rather than measure it.
3. A comment is what a player chose to write, not a measurement. Players who did not mention the camera may still have had trouble with it, and players who mentioned it may have been mildly irritated. Report “12 of 60 comments mentioned the camera”, and check it against telemetry or observation, such as how often the camera was reset.
4. Name the factor, what it might change, and whether you checked it. For example: “Experienced players may navigate better whichever build they play. We checked the wrong-turns result within each cohort.” Any specific factor, checked or not, is better than “other factors”.

title: Combining Evidence
text:
Summary

Telemetry says what happened, observation how it unfolded, self-report what players experienced. Choose measures from at least two for every question that matters.
Observation is evidence only when it is recorded the same way for every player: use an observation sheet with a fixed list of behaviours.
Code comments with a short, written codebook; apply it in R with case_when() and grepl(); check a sample by hand; report counts as counts of comments.
Quote to illustrate a pattern, never to be the pattern.
Triangulate. Agreement makes a finding strong; disagreement tells you what each source is really measuring.
Write limitations that are specific, say what they might change, and say whether you checked.








Key term
Meaning




Triangulation
Checking a finding against more than one source of evidence


Observation sheet
A fixed list of behaviours recorded the same way for every player


Code
A category given to a piece of free text


Codebook
The list of codes, what each means, and an example of each


Limitation
A specific weakness that could change the conclusion, stated by the author

title: Combining Evidence
text:
Reflective Questions

Which of your team’s measures would you trust most for what happened, and which for how it felt? Are they the same?
Your comments say players loved a feature that the telemetry says almost nobody used. Write the sentence you would put in the Discussion.
What three behaviours would you put on an observation sheet for your next playtest, and why those?
Which of your own limitations would most change your Conclusion if it turned out to matter?

title: Relationships and Correlation
text:
Workflow
  
    Question
    Measure
    Collect
    Clean
    Describe
    Compare/Relate
    Interpret
    Act

title: Relationships and Correlation
Relationships and Correlation
text:
Why This Matters for Playtesting
Comparing two builds was a controlled question: the team chose who played which. Most of what a playtest records is not controlled. Awareness, deaths, experience, difficulty ratings: they all arrive together, and they all move together, because they all come from the same players.
A relationship is a lead, not a finding. “Players with high awareness scored more” is true in the Tidebreak data, and it is tempting to read it as “awareness causes score, so buff awareness”. The data cannot say that. Better players may simply be more aware and score more. The difference between those two readings decides whether a balance patch helps or does nothing, and only careful reasoning, not more computation, tells them apart (rule 7).
For your project: by now your team has its own playtest data. This page is written so that every step works on it. The clinic lab ends with a correlation matrix of your own measures.

title: Relationships and Correlation
text:
Seeing a Relationship: the Scatterplot
A scatterplot draws one point per observation, with one variable on each axis. Do players who die more rate the game as more difficult?

ggplot(sessions, aes(x = deaths, y = difficulty)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0.15, colour = pal$line, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Deaths in the session", y = "Difficulty rating (1–7)")







Figure 1: Players who died more rated the game as harder, with a lot of variation. Points are jittered slightly because both variables are whole numbers.





geom_jitter() is geom_point() with a little random nudge, so that sessions with the same values do not sit on top of each other. Read a scatterplot for three things:

Direction. Do the points rise from left to right (positive: more of one, more of the other) or fall (negative)? Here they rise.
Form. Do they follow a straight line, a curve, or no pattern at all? Here, roughly a line.
Strength. How tightly do they cluster around that form? Here, loosely: plenty of players died often and still rated the game easy.

In a report you would write: “Players who died more rated the game as harder, though with wide variation between players.”

title: Relationships and Correlation
text:
Measuring a Relationship: Correlation
The correlation coefficient, r, puts a number on direction and strength for a straight-line relationship. It runs from −1 to +1:








Figure 2: What correlations look like. At ±0.2 there is barely a pattern; at ±0.9 the points form a tight band.






+1: a perfect rising line. −1: a perfect falling line.
0: no straight-line relationship.
The further from 0, the more tightly the points follow a line.

cor() computes it:

cor(sessions$deaths, sessions$difficulty)

[1] 0.5792729


r = 0.58: a clear positive relationship with a lot of scatter, which is what Figure 1 showed.
Context decides what counts as strong. There is no universal cut-off. Between two measurements of the same thing, such as two raters scoring the same session, 0.6 would be worryingly low. Between a single rating and a match outcome shaped by teammates, opponents and luck, 0.5 is large. Say what the number means for the question, not just whether it is “strong”.

Pearson or Spearman?
The correlation above is Pearson’s, the default. It measures how well the points follow a straight line, and a few extreme values can pull it around.
Spearman’s correlation ranks each variable first, then correlates the ranks. It asks a simpler question: when one goes up, does the other tend to go up? It does not need a straight line, and an outlier is just the highest rank, so it cannot drag the result.

cor(sessions$deaths, sessions$difficulty, method = "spearman")

[1] 0.5731608


0.57, almost the same as Pearson’s here, because the relationship is roughly straight with no wild values.
For now, use this rule:







Use
When




Pearson
Both variables are measurements or counts, the scatterplot looks roughly straight, and nothing sits far from the rest


Spearman
Either variable is a rating (ordinal), the relationship curves but keeps going one way, or a few extreme values sit apart



Playtest data is full of ratings, so Spearman is often the safer choice. If the two disagree a lot, draw the scatterplot: something is bending or pulling the line.

title: Relationships and Correlation
section: Many Relationships at Once: the Correlation Matrix
text:
Many Relationships at Once: the Correlation Matrix
A playtest records many measures, and the first useful question is often which of them go together? A correlation matrix answers it in one table: the correlation of every measure with every other.
Pick 3 to 5 measures that matter to your question, not every column you have. For Tidebreak’s navigation and difficulty questions:

sessions |>
  select(deaths, wrong_turns, difficulty, enjoyment, session_minutes) |>
  cor(method = "spearman") |>
  round(2)

                deaths wrong_turns difficulty enjoyment session_minutes
deaths            1.00       -0.03       0.57     -0.20           -0.02
wrong_turns      -0.03        1.00      -0.09     -0.03            0.04
difficulty        0.57       -0.09       1.00     -0.33            0.15
enjoyment        -0.20       -0.03      -0.33      1.00            0.23
session_minutes  -0.02        0.04       0.15      0.23            1.00


select() keeps the five columns, cor() of a whole table correlates every pair, and round(2) makes it readable. Spearman, because difficulty and enjoyment are 1–7 ratings.
How to read it:

The diagonal is all 1s. Every measure correlates perfectly with itself. Ignore it.
It is symmetric. The value in row deaths, column difficulty is the same as row difficulty, column deaths. Read one triangle.
Read one row at a time and look for the values furthest from 0.

What this one says:

deaths and difficulty go together most strongly, 0.57: players who die more rate the game harder. Telemetry and self-report agree.
difficulty and enjoyment move in opposite directions, -0.33: players who found it harder enjoyed it less.
wrong_turns is close to 0 with everything, between -0.09 and 0.04. Getting lost does not go with dying, with rating the game hard, or with enjoying it less.

That last line is the interesting one, and the next section explains why.
Draw before you trust the matrix. Each number stands in for a scatterplot you have not drawn. Base R’s pairs() draws them all at once:

pairs(sessions[, c("deaths", "wrong_turns", "difficulty", "enjoyment",
                   "session_minutes")],
      pch = 19, cex = 0.4, col = adjustcolor(pal$line, alpha.f = 0.4))







Figure 3: Every pair of the five measures as a scatterplot. Deaths against difficulty is the clearest pattern; wrong turns show none against anything.





You do not need to memorise this: pairs() is a quick check, not a figure for the report.
For your project: choose the 3–5 measures your design question depends on, build their matrix, and read it row by row. The strongest relationship is a lead to look at, and the one you expected but did not find is often the finding.

title: Relationships and Correlation
text:
Telemetry, Observation and Self-Report Together
The three sources of evidence from Planning a Playtest answer different questions, and relating them is where correlation earns its keep.
When they agree, the finding is stronger. Deaths (telemetry) and the difficulty rating (self-report) go together: what happened and what players felt point the same way.
When they disagree, there is something to find. Build B cut wrong turns from 8.9 to 5.5 per session on average. So do players who got lost more rate the level as harder to navigate? The survey item “the level was easy to navigate” (level_navigable) is in a separate file, so join it on first:

joined <- sessions |>
  left_join(survey, by = "session_id")

cor(joined$wrong_turns, joined$level_navigable, method = "spearman")

[1] 0.05151128

joined |>
  group_by(build) |>
  summarise(mean_wrong_turns = mean(wrong_turns),
            mean_navigable   = mean(level_navigable))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  build mean_wrong_turns mean_navigable
  <chr>            <dbl>          <dbl>
1 A                 8.92           3.2 
2 B                 5.52           3.23


left_join() adds the survey columns to each session, matched on session_id.
The correlation is 0.05: no relationship. And the builds rated navigation almost identically, 3.2 against 3.23, even though Build A’s players got lost far more. Players did not notice that they were lost. The telemetry saw a navigation problem the self-report did not.
That is a finding, and it changes what you do with each source. A navigation survey on its own would have said the level was fine. Wrong turns on their own say what happened but not whether players minded. Observation is what would connect them: watching where players hesitate or backtrack, and whether they seem to know it.
In a report you would write: “Build A players made more wrong turns, but rated the level as no harder to navigate (Spearman r = 0.05 between wrong turns and the navigation rating). Players appear not to notice when they are lost, so self-reported navigation is not a reliable check on this level.”

title: Relationships and Correlation
text:
What Correlation Cannot See
A single number cannot describe a picture. In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe published four small datasets that make the point. They have almost identical means, SDs and correlations, and they look nothing alike:


Show the code
quartet <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:4, function(i) {
  data.frame(set = paste("Set", i),
             x = anscombe[[paste0("x", i)]], y = anscombe[[paste0("y", i)]])
}))

ggplot(quartet, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(colour = pal$line, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = pal$highlight, linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ set, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)








Figure 4: Anscombe’s quartet: four datasets with the same correlation, about 0.82, and four different stories.





Only Set 1 is what r = 0.82 suggests. Set 2 is a curve, which r describes badly. In Set 3, one outlier drags the line away from an otherwise perfect fit. In Set 4, a single point creates the entire relationship.
Always draw the scatterplot before quoting r (rule 4). Correlation sees only straight lines, is moved by single extreme points, and, as the next two sections show, cannot see groups.

title: Relationships and Correlation
text:
Correlation Is Not Causation
When two variables move together, there are always several explanations, and “one causes the other” is only one of them:







Explanation
Awareness and score




A causes B
Being aware of the map makes players score more


B causes A
Players who are scoring well have more time to look around


Something else causes both
Experienced players are both more aware and better at everything


Chance
In a small sample, unrelated measures can line up by luck



A playtest observes; it does not intervene. Only a test in which you change one variable and watch the other, such as giving half the players a better minimap at random, can separate the first explanation from the rest. Until then, write “is associated with”, never “causes” or “drives”.

title: Relationships and Correlation
text:
Confounding: Look Within Groups
A confounding variable is a third variable that drives both of the variables you are comparing, creating or hiding a relationship between them.






flowchart TD
  E["Experience<br/>(cohort)"] --> A["Awareness"]
  E --> S["Score"]
  A -.->|"what you observe"| S
  class E accent




Figure 5: A confounder drives both variables. The relationship you see between them may come partly or entirely from it.





Which abilities go with score?

sessions |>
  select(accuracy, mobility, survivability, objective_control, support,
         awareness, shots_fired) |>
  cor(sessions$score) |>
  round(2)

                   [,1]
accuracy           0.03
mobility           0.29
survivability     -0.07
objective_control  0.09
support            0.15
awareness          0.59
shots_fired        0.05


Awareness is the strongest, at 0.59. Shots fired, the statistic everyone assumes matters, is 0.05: no relationship at all.
Experience is a candidate confounder for awareness and score. Veterans average 75.6 awareness against 57.3 for Novices, and a median score of 1664 against 1281. Some of the awareness–score relationship is experience. Check within each cohort:

sessions |>
  group_by(cohort) |>
  summarise(n = n(), r = cor(awareness, score))

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  cohort      n     r
  <chr>   <int> <dbl>
1 Novice     33 0.539
2 Regular    53 0.477
3 Veteran    34 0.445


From 0.45 to 0.54 within each cohort: experience is part of the story, not all of it. That is how you check a suspected confounder: split by it, and see whether the relationship holds inside each group. It is group_by() and summarise() again, with cor() as the summary.

When the relationship reverses
Sometimes splitting by the confounder does not just weaken a relationship; it reverses it. That is Simpson’s paradox, and Tidebreak has a clear case. You do not need to be able to produce this figure; it is here because it is the most memorable demonstration of confounding there is.
Across all players, mobility and survivability have a correlation of -0.66: faster players are more fragile. Within each archetype:


Show the code
both <- rbind(
  data.frame(sessions[, c("mobility", "survivability", "archetype")], panel = "All players"),
  data.frame(sessions[, c("mobility", "survivability", "archetype")], panel = "By archetype")
)
ggplot(both, aes(mobility, survivability)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = ifelse(panel == "All players", "All", archetype)), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(data = subset(both, panel == "All players"), method = "lm",
              se = FALSE, colour = "black") +
  geom_smooth(data = subset(both, panel == "By archetype"),
              aes(colour = archetype), method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(All = "grey60", Duelist = "#3a5f8a",
                                 Engineer = "#6c9a3c", Scout = "#b22222",
                                 Sentinel = "#8a5a9c"),
                      breaks = c("Duelist", "Engineer", "Scout", "Sentinel")) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  labs(x = "Mobility rating", y = "Survivability rating", colour = "Archetype")








Figure 6: Across all players (left) faster means more fragile. Within every archetype (right) the trend rises: the falling line is the gap between archetypes.






sessions |>
  group_by(archetype) |>
  summarise(r = cor(mobility, survivability))

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  archetype     r
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 Duelist   0.302
2 Engineer  0.512
3 Scout     0.465
4 Sentinel  0.598


Within every archetype the correlation is positive, from 0.3 to 0.6. The overall falling trend is the gap between archetypes: Scouts are built fast and fragile, Sentinels slow and tough. Within any one archetype, better players are better at both. Archetype is the confounder, and ignoring it reverses the conclusion. A patch that “makes fast players more fragile” would punish exactly the players who are playing their role well.
For your project: before you report any relationship, split it by the one or two groupings most likely to matter in your game: build, level, character or experience.

title: Relationships and Correlation
text:
Two Categorical Variables
When both variables are categories, correlation is the wrong tool. Count every combination, then turn each group’s counts into shares, so that groups of different sizes compare fairly. Do more experienced players quit in frustration less?

sessions |>
  count(cohort, quit_reason) |>
  group_by(cohort) |>
  mutate(share = round(n / sum(n), 2))

# A tibble: 11 × 4
# Groups:   cohort [3]
   cohort  quit_reason         n share
   <chr>   <chr>           <int> <dbl>
 1 Novice  Completed test     23  0.7 
 2 Novice  Frustrated          6  0.18
 3 Novice  Lost interest       3  0.09
 4 Novice  Technical fault     1  0.03
 5 Regular Completed test     27  0.51
 6 Regular Frustrated         14  0.26
 7 Regular Lost interest       8  0.15
 8 Regular Technical fault     4  0.08
 9 Veteran Completed test     19  0.56
10 Veteran Frustrated          5  0.15
11 Veteran Lost interest      10  0.29



ggplot(sessions, aes(x = cohort, fill = quit_reason)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x * 100, "%")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey80", "#b22222", "#9bb0c9", "grey40")) +
  labs(x = "Cohort", y = "Share of sessions", fill = "How the session ended")







Figure 7: Regulars quit in frustration most often; Veterans more often simply lost interest. Each bar is one cohort, scaled to 100%.





position = "fill" scales every bar to 100%. Not in a straight line: Regulars quit in frustration most often, 26% of their sessions, against 18% for Novices and 15% for Veterans.

title: Relationships and Correlation
text:
Critiquing a Playtest
Every one of these ideas comes together when a conclusion is drawn from data that cannot support it. Two scenarios to take apart.

A team adds an optional minimap. Players who turned it on scored 22% higher than players who left it off. The team makes the minimap mandatory.
The new build was tested on Friday evening with fans recruited from the studio Discord; the old build on Monday morning with first-year students. Enjoyment was 1.5 points higher for the new build, p < 0.001. The team reports that the new build is more enjoyable.







NoteShow answers






Players chose whether to use the minimap, so the two groups differ in more than the minimap. Experienced, engaged players are more likely to explore the options menu and more likely to score well: a confounder. The 22% may be entirely skill. To know what the minimap does, assign it at random, or have every player try both, counterbalanced (Planning a Playtest).
Build is confounded with everything else that differed: the players (committed fans against strangers), the time of day, and probably the room and who ran the session. Any of them could produce the gap. The p-value says the gap is unlikely to be chance; it says nothing about which of the differences caused it. The fix is to recruit one group and assign builds at random within it, at the same times, in the same room.

title: Relationships and Correlation
text:
Worked Example
Should we buff awareness? The balance designer has seen that awareness is the strongest predictor of score and proposes raising every archetype’s base awareness.
Step 1: look. A scatterplot of score against awareness shows a clear rising relationship, with a cluster of sessions far below the rest: the Sentinel collapses from Describing Variables.
Step 2: measure. r = 0.59, the strongest of the ability ratings. Shots fired, the obvious candidate, is 0.05.
Step 3: ask what else could explain it. Experience: Veterans have more of both. Within each cohort the relationship weakens but survives (0.45 to 0.54), so experience is part of the story. And a player’s awareness rating may measure skill as much as cause it: good players notice more because they are good.
Step 4: conclude. The data shows an association, and a fairly strong one. It does not show that raising awareness would raise score.
What should the team do? Run a test, not a patch: give half the players a feature that raises awareness, such as a clearer minimap or audio cues, at random, and compare score between the groups. That turns the relationship into a Stage 2 comparison, which can show cause.

title: Relationships and Correlation
text:
Interpretation Guidance
What the data shows. Score rises with awareness, r = 0.59, across 120 sessions, and the relationship survives within each cohort.
What the analysis suggests. Awareness, or whatever awareness ratings reflect, matters to how a match goes. Experience explains part of the relationship but not all of it.
What can legitimately be concluded. An association, not a cause. A design change aimed at awareness is worth testing; it is not yet supported as a fix.
Use the right verbs. “Is associated with”, “goes with”, “predicts” for relationships in observed data. “Causes”, “drives”, “improves” only after an experiment that changed one variable on purpose.
Going further: fitting the line itself, with slope, R² and residuals, and reading what the residuals tell you, is on Regression.

title: Relationships and Correlation
text:
Common Mistakes
Quoting r without the scatterplot. Anscombe’s four datasets share a correlation and nothing else (rule 4).
Reading correlation as cause. Two things moving together has at least four explanations. Name the alternatives before choosing one.
Ignoring groups. A relationship across groups can vanish or reverse within them. Split by the obvious confounders, such as archetype, cohort or build.
Calling r “strong” or “weak” without context. Say what it means for the question.
Putting every column in the matrix. A 20 × 20 matrix has 190 correlations and some will look strong by luck. Choose the 3–5 that answer your question.
Using Pearson on ratings without checking. For 1–7 ratings, use Spearman, or at least check that the two agree.
Using correlation on categories. Two categorical variables need counts and shares, not cor().

title: Relationships and Correlation
text:
Practice
Each takes two or three minutes.

Predict. Before computing it: is the correlation between kills and score closer to 0, 0.5 or 0.9? Then check.
Compute. Build a Spearman correlation matrix of kills, deaths, time_alive_s and score. Which measure goes with score most strongly?
Critique. “Wrong turns correlate at -0.07 with enjoyment, so getting lost does not affect how much players enjoy the game.” What is wrong with that conclusion?
Decide. The correlation between deaths and difficulty is about the same in both builds. Check it with group_by(). Why is that worth knowing before you use deaths as a stand-in for “how hard players found it”?







NoteShow answers





1.

cor(sessions$kills, sessions$score)

[1] 0.06510531


Close to 0, 0.07, which surprises most people. A number you were sure about is exactly the one to check.
2.

sessions |>
  select(kills, deaths, time_alive_s, score) |>
  cor(method = "spearman") |>
  round(2)

             kills deaths time_alive_s score
kills         1.00   0.06        -0.19  0.10
deaths        0.06   1.00        -0.56 -0.53
time_alive_s -0.19  -0.56         1.00  0.32
score         0.10  -0.53         0.32  1.00


Read the score row, and look at the size, not the sign. Deaths go with score most strongly, -0.53: negative, so fewer deaths, more score. Time alive is next, 0.32. Kills barely register, 0.1. In Tidebreak, staying alive is what scores, not killing.
3. A correlation near zero means no straight-line relationship across all sessions. It does not rule out a curve, a relationship within one build or cohort that is cancelled out by another, or an effect on a different outcome: players who got lost may have quit. Draw the scatterplot, split by build, and look at quit reason too before concluding anything.
4.

sessions |>
  group_by(build) |>
  summarise(r = cor(deaths, difficulty, method = "spearman"))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  build     r
  <chr> <dbl>
1 A     0.585
2 B     0.581


The relationship holds in each build, so it is not produced by mixing two different builds together. That makes deaths a more trustworthy stand-in for felt difficulty in either build, although it is still only a stand-in: plenty of players died often and rated the game easy.

title: Relationships and Correlation
text:
Summary

A scatterplot shows a relationship’s direction, form and strength. Draw it first.
Correlation, from −1 to +1, measures how two things move together. Pearson for straight-line relationships between measurements; Spearman for ratings, curves that keep going one way, or outliers.
A correlation matrix of 3–5 chosen measures shows which go together. Read one row at a time, and draw the pairs before trusting it.
Telemetry and self-report can disagree: Tidebreak’s players got lost without rating the level as harder to navigate. The disagreement is a finding.
Correlation is not causation: the reverse direction, a third variable or chance can produce the same pattern.
A confounder drives both variables. Check by splitting into groups; Simpson’s paradox is when the relationship reverses inside them.








Key term
Meaning




Scatterplot
One point per observation, for two numeric variables


Correlation (r)
−1 to +1: how strongly two variables move together


Pearson
The default correlation: how well the points follow a straight line


Spearman
Correlation of ranks: does one go up when the other does?


Correlation matrix
The correlation of every chosen measure with every other


Causation
One variable changing another; needs an experiment to show


Confounding variable
A third variable that drives both variables you are comparing


Simpson’s paradox
A relationship that reverses when the data is split into groups

text:
