title: R from First Principles
R from First Principles
text:
Why This Matters for Playtesting
A playtest produces a few thousand rows of telemetry, a survey export and a frame log, and next week it produces them again for the new build. The question is not whether you can analyse them once. It is whether you can analyse them again, identically, in a minute, when the build changes.
That is the case for writing your analysis as code. A spreadsheet records the answer; a script records how you got it, so it can be checked, repeated on next week’s data, and handed to a teammate who gets exactly the same result.

title: R from First Principles
text:
Why R?
R is a language built for data. Where most languages treat a table of numbers as something you have to build, R starts there. Taking the mean of a column, counting categories or drawing a histogram is one line:

hist(sessions$session_minutes, col = pal$fill, border = "white",
     main = "", xlab = "Session length (minutes)")







Figure 1: One line of R draws the distribution of every Tidebreak session length.





Against a spreadsheet. Spreadsheets are fine for looking at a small table and poor at everything this course needs. They hide the steps, so nobody can check how a number was made. They invite editing the data by hand, so the original is lost. And they have to be redone, click by click, when new data arrives. A widely cited 2010 economics paper by Reinhart and Rogoff was later found to contain a spreadsheet formula that left five countries out of an average, an error nobody spotted for three years because the steps were hidden in cells. Code does not prevent mistakes, but it leaves them where someone can find them.
Against Python. Python is the other obvious choice and a perfectly good one. R is used here because its statistics and plotting are built in rather than added, and because Quarto and R work together with no setup. Everything you learn transfers: a data frame, a vector and a grouped summary are the same ideas in both.

Base R and the tidyverse
R comes with a large set of built-in functions, called base R. On top of it, most modern R uses the tidyverse: a family of packages (readr, dplyr, ggplot2 and others) with a consistent, readable style.
This course uses both, with one way to do each job:

Handling data: the tidyverse. read_csv() to load it, then verbs such as count(), filter() and summarise(), chained with the pipe |>.
Summary statistics: base R’s mean(), median(), sd() and friends, which the tidyverse uses too.
Plots: base R in Stages 1 and 2 (hist(), boxplot(), plot()), which are quick and good for looking while you think. ggplot2 arrives in Stage 3, for figures other people will read.

You do not need to memorise this: code you find online will often do the same jobs in other ways. Where that matters, these notes show you what the other way looks like, so you can read it, and say that you do not need to write it.

title: R from First Principles
text:
Where You Write R
There are four places R code lives, and each has a job.






flowchart LR
  subgraph PROJECT["Project folder"]
    direction TB
    S["Script<br/>analysis.R"]
    Q["Quarto document<br/>report.qmd"]
    D[("data/<br/>CSV files")]
  end
  C["Console"]
  S -->|"run a line<br/>Ctrl+Enter"| C
  Q -->|"run a chunk"| C
  Q -->|"Render"| H["Web page<br/>report.html"]
  D -.->|"read_csv()"| S
  D -.->|"read_csv()"| Q
  class C,H accent




Figure 2: Try things in the console; keep them in a script or Quarto document, inside one project folder.





The console is where R runs. Type a line, press Enter, see the result. It is for trying things out, and nothing typed there is kept.
A script (.R file) is a text file of R code. You write lines in it and send them to the console with Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on macOS) in both VS Code and RStudio. A script is your analysis: if it is not in the script, it did not happen.
A Quarto document (.qmd file) mixes prose and R code. Rendering it runs every chunk in order and produces a web page with the text, code, numbers and plots together. Your playtest report will be one of these; the full story is in Stage 4, Interpreting and Reporting Evidence.
A project is the folder that holds everything: scripts, documents and a data/ folder. Working inside the project means R looks for files relative to that folder, which is why every path in these notes starts data/.
For your project: make one project folder for your team’s playtest analysis now, with a data/ folder inside it. Every export from every playtest goes there, unedited. You will thank yourself in March.

title: R from First Principles
text:
Values and Objects
At its simplest, R is a calculator.

2 + 3

[1] 5

1370 / 4

[1] 342.5

2^10

[1] 1024


The [1] in front of each answer is not part of it. It is R telling you this line of output starts with the first value; you will see why it matters when an answer has many values.
To keep a value, give it a name with the assignment arrow <-, read aloud as “gets”:

score <- 1370
score

[1] 1370

score * 2

[1] 2740


score is now an object: a named value that lives in your R session until you close it or overwrite it. Names are case-sensitive (Score is a different object), cannot start with a number, and should say what the value is. session_minutes is a good name; x2 is not.






NoteGoing further: <- or =?





score = 1370 also works, and R programmers argue about which is better. These notes use <- for assignment and keep = for naming arguments inside a function call, such as mean(x, na.rm = TRUE). That way, = always means “this argument gets this value” and <- always means “this object gets this value”. In RStudio, Alt+- types the arrow; VS Code can be given the same shortcut in its keyboard settings.

title: R from First Principles
text:
Types
Every value has a type. class() tells you which.

class(1370)

[1] "numeric"

class("Scout")

[1] "character"

class(TRUE)

[1] "logical"





Type
What it holds
Examples




numeric
numbers, whole or decimal
1370, 24.6


character
text, always in quotes
"Scout", "S001"


logical
TRUE or FALSE
the answer to any comparison



Comparisons produce logicals. == tests equality (a single = is not a comparison), != tests inequality, and <, >, <=, >= work as you would expect:

score > 1500

[1] FALSE

score == 1370

[1] TRUE

"Scout" == "scout"

[1] FALSE


The last one is FALSE because text comparison is case-sensitive, which matters a great deal when you come to clean real data.
R does not make you declare types. If you come from C#, this is the first big difference: there is no int score = 1370;. R works the type out from the value, and it will convert between types without asking. That is convenient until it is not:

as.numeric("24.6")

[1] 24.6

as.numeric("twenty")

Warning: NAs introduced by coercion


[1] NA


The second line returns NA, R’s marker for a missing value, with a warning. It does not stop. A column of numbers with one typo in it can quietly become a column of text, and every calculation on it then fails or misleads. Checking types is the first thing you do with any new data.






NoteGoing further: integers





R has a separate integer type for whole numbers, written with an L: 4L. You will rarely need to create one, but you will see it: base R’s read.csv() stores whole-number columns as integers, while readr’s read_csv() stores all numbers as numeric (printed <dbl>, for double precision). For analysis the difference almost never matters.

title: R from First Principles
text:
Vectors
In C#, a single number is the basic unit and a collection is something you build. In R it is the other way round. The basic unit is the vector: an ordered collection of values, all of the same type. A single number is just a vector of length one, which is what the [1] was telling you.
Build a vector with c(), for combine:

deaths <- c(4, 2, 7, 3, 0, 5)
deaths

[1] 4 2 7 3 0 5

length(deaths)

[1] 6










Figure 3: A vector holds values in order, each with a position. R counts positions from 1.





Arithmetic works on every element at once. This is called vectorisation, and it replaces most of the loops you would write in C#:

deaths + 1

[1] 5 3 8 4 1 6

deaths * 10

[1] 40 20 70 30  0 50


Summary functions collapse a vector to one value:

sum(deaths)

[1] 21

mean(deaths)

[1] 3.5

max(deaths)

[1] 7


A comparison on a vector gives one logical per element, and because R counts TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0, summing or averaging that vector counts it:

deaths > 2

[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE

sum(deaths > 2)

[1] 4

mean(deaths > 2)

[1] 0.6666667


sum(deaths > 2) is “how many sessions had more than two deaths”; mean(deaths > 2) is “what proportion did”. You need to know this one: it produces a large share of the numbers in a playtest report.
Every element has the same type. Mix them and R converts everything to the most general type, usually character:

c(1, "two", 3)

[1] "1"   "two" "3"  


The numbers are now text, in quotes. This is the same silent conversion as before, and it is why a vector, and every column of a table, holds one type only.

title: R from First Principles
text:
Indexing
Square brackets pull elements out of a vector. If you write C# or C++, the one mistake you will make is this: R counts from 1, not 0.

deaths[1]

[1] 4

deaths[c(3, 5)]

[1] 7 0

deaths[deaths > 2]

[1] 4 7 3 5










Figure 4: The same vector indexed three ways. A condition inside the brackets keeps the elements where it is TRUE.





The last one is the important one. A logical index keeps the elements where a condition holds. It is the same idea as filtering rows of a table, which you will do with filter() in Stage 2.
For now, that is all the indexing you need to write. You will see square brackets used on whole tables in code online; the box below shows what they mean.






NoteGoing further: indexing a table with [rows, columns]





Base R slices a data frame with [rows, columns]. Leave a side empty to mean “all of them”; the comma separates rows from columns.

sessions[2, c("session_id", "deaths")]

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  session_id deaths
  <chr>       <dbl>
1 S002            2

nrow(sessions[sessions$deaths > 8, ])

[1] 0


The second line keeps the rows where deaths is above 8 and counts them. You only need to recognise this. In these notes the same jobs are done with filter() and select(), which read more like the question you are asking.

title: R from First Principles
text:
Functions and Arguments
A function takes inputs, called arguments, and returns a result. You have already used several: c(), class(), sum(), mean().
Arguments have names and an order. args() shows both:

args(round)

function (x, digits = 0, ...) 
NULL


round() takes x, the number, and digits, which defaults to 0. You can supply arguments by position, in the order the function declares them, or by name, in any order:

round(3.14159, 2)

[1] 3.14

round(x = 3.14159, digits = 2)

[1] 3.14

round(digits = 2, x = 3.14159)

[1] 3.14


All three give the same answer. Without names, position is everything, and swapping the values changes the meaning:

round(2, 3.14159)

[1] 2


That rounds 2 to three decimal places. Pass the main input by position and everything else by name: mean(deaths, na.rm = TRUE). It reads well, and it lets you skip arguments you are happy to leave at their defaults.
Every function has a help page. Type ?round in the console. The page lists every argument, its default, what the function returns, and examples at the bottom, which are usually the quickest way to understand it.






NoteGoing further: writing your own function





You can define functions with function(). This one turns a logical vector into a percentage, with a default of one decimal place:

pct <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  round(100 * mean(x), digits)
}

pct(deaths > 2)

[1] 66.7

pct(deaths > 2, digits = 0)

[1] 67


The last expression in the body is the return value; there is no return keyword needed. You will not need to write functions for the labs, but it is how R programmers stop repeating themselves.

title: R from First Principles
text:
Missing Values
NA means a value should be there but was not recorded: a session length the logger lost, a survey question the player skipped. It is not zero and not empty. It means unknown.

minutes <- c(12.9, 24.6, NA, 18.8)
mean(minutes)

[1] NA


Any calculation involving an unknown is unknown. R will not guess. Tell it to leave the missing values out with na.rm = TRUE, and find them with is.na():

mean(minutes, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 18.76667

is.na(minutes)

[1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE

sum(is.na(minutes))

[1] 1


sum(is.na(x)) is the count of missing values: the same “sum a logical to count it” trick as before. Before you drop missing values, ask why they are missing. Sometimes the pattern of what is missing is itself a finding, which is the subject of Cleaning and Transforming.

title: R from First Principles
text:
Data Frames
A playtest table is a data frame: a set of vectors of equal length, one per column, side by side. Each column has one type; each row is one observation.






flowchart LR
  V1["session<br/>S001 S002 S003"] --> DF[("data frame<br/>3 rows × 3 columns")]
  V2["archetype<br/>Scout Tank Scout"] --> DF
  V3["deaths<br/>4 2 7"] --> DF
  class DF accent




Figure 5: A data frame is a set of equal-length vectors, one per column.





You can build a small one by hand from vectors, which is handy for trying an idea out:

mini <- data.frame(
  session   = c("S001", "S002", "S003", "S004"),
  archetype = c("Scout", "Tank", "Scout", "Support"),
  deaths    = c(4, 2, 7, 3)
)
mini

  session archetype deaths
1    S001     Scout      4
2    S002      Tank      2
3    S003     Scout      7
4    S004   Support      3


$ pulls out one column, as a vector, and everything from the Vectors section works on it:

mini$deaths

[1] 4 2 7 3

mean(mini$deaths)

[1] 4

sum(mini$deaths > 3)

[1] 2


In practice you rarely type a data frame in. You read one from a file.

title: R from First Principles
text:
Packages and Reading Data
A package is a bundle of extra functions someone else has written. Using one is two steps:

install.packages("tidyverse")   # once per computer: downloads and installs it
library(readr)                  # every session: makes its functions available

Installing is like adding a library to a project; loading is like the using statement at the top of a C# file. Forget the library() call and R reports could not find function, which is the most common error in the first week.
Reading a CSV is one line with readr’s read_csv():

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
sessions <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_sessions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

The path is relative to the project folder. read_csv() returns a tibble, the tidyverse’s version of a data frame. Everything above works on it unchanged.
Look before you do anything else. glimpse(), from dplyr, shows the size of the table and one line per column: its name, its type and its first few values.

glimpse(sessions)

Rows: 120
Columns: 26
$ session_id        <chr> "S001", "S002", "S003", "S004", "S005", "S006", "S00…
$ player_id         <chr> "P01", "P02", "P03", "P04", "P05", "P06", "P07", "P0…
$ cohort            <chr> "Regular", "Veteran", "Regular", "Novice", "Veteran"…
$ archetype         <chr> "Scout", "Scout", "Scout", "Scout", "Scout", "Scout"…
$ build             <chr> "A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A…
$ accuracy          <dbl> 55, 54, 48, 35, 67, 51, 57, 42, 51, 47, 56, 40, 60, …
$ mobility          <dbl> 84, 91, 89, 80, 97, 90, 95, 73, 86, 86, 84, 83, 92, …
$ survivability     <dbl> 48, 52, 42, 35, 56, 41, 45, 30, 35, 40, 49, 27, 46, …
$ objective_control <dbl> 39, 66, 43, 47, 55, 45, 53, 39, 51, 49, 52, 35, 52, …
$ support           <dbl> 52, 46, 52, 28, 38, 56, 47, 46, 34, 51, 55, 40, 53, …

$ kills             <dbl> 7, 5, 5, 7, 12, 7, 6, 7, 7, 10, 9, 5, 10, 10, 5, 8, …
$ deaths            <dbl> 4, 2, 2, 4, 3, 5, 4, 4, 3, 4, 3, 5, 5, 5, 5, 4, 4, 2…
$ objectives        <dbl> 0, 2, 4, 2, 4, 4, 3, 2, 3, 3, 4, 1, 1, 1, 2, 4, 1, 2…
$ shots_fired       <dbl> 148, 140, 190, 92, 143, 149, 143, 126, 138, 137, 118…
$ time_alive_s      <dbl> 98, 105, 115, 80, 121, 115, 118, 99, 103, 71, 143, 7…
$ distance_m        <dbl> 571, 520, 533, 349, 542, 566, 572, 308, 560, 451, 40…
$ session_minutes   <dbl> 12.9, 24.6, 12.5, 18.8, 18.7, 25.3, 11.5, 27.0, 14.4…
$ quit_reason       <chr> "Frustrated", "Lost interest", "Frustrated", "Lost i…
$ wrong_turns       <dbl> 8, 4, 9, 7, 10, 9, 9, 2, 11, 2, 3, 7, 5, 6, 8, 2, 8,…
$ items_collected   <dbl> 3, 5, 2, 3, 4, 0, 5, 6, 7, 5, 2, 6, 3, 0, 0, 6, 3, 7…
$ completed         <lgl> TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FAL…
$ difficulty        <dbl> 4, 4, 3, 3, 3, 5, 4, 5, 4, 5, 3, 6, 5, 5, 6, 5, 4, 4…
$ enjoyment         <dbl> 2, 5, 6, 4, 3, 3, 4, 3, 4, 3, 5, 3, 4, 4, 3, 4, 3, 3…
$ comment           <chr> "Could not tell where I was meant to go.", "The sign…


120 rows, 26 columns. <chr> is character and <dbl> is numeric. Whether those types match what each column means is a separate question, and the subject of Data, Variables and Types.
You will also see str(), head() and summary() doing similar jobs in other people’s code. You do not need to write them.

title: R from First Principles
text:
The Pipe
Most analysis is a short chain of steps: take the data, do this, then that. The pipe, |>, writes the chain in the order it happens. Read it aloud as “and then”:

sessions |> count(build)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  build     n
  <chr> <int>
1 A        60
2 B        60


“Take sessions, and then count the rows for each build.” The pipe passes whatever is on its left in as the first argument of the function on its right, so this is exactly count(sessions, build). With one step there is no difference; with four steps, the piped version still reads top to bottom.

sessions |> count(build, quit_reason)

# A tibble: 8 × 3
  build quit_reason         n
  <chr> <chr>           <int>
1 A     Completed test     31
2 A     Frustrated         20
3 A     Lost interest       7
4 A     Technical fault     2
5 B     Completed test     38
6 B     Frustrated          5
7 B     Lost interest      14
8 B     Technical fault     3


Two columns in count() counts every combination: how each build’s sessions ended. You will add more verbs to the chain as the course goes on: group_by() and summarise() in Describing Variables, and filter(), select() and mutate() in Stage 2.
You will also see %>% in code online. It is an older pipe that does the same job. Read it as |>.

title: R from First Principles
text:
Reading Error Messages
R’s error messages are terse, but they nearly always name the problem. Read the error before changing anything. Here are the ones you will meet most, produced live:

mean(sesions$score)

Error:
! object 'sesions' not found


object not found: a typo in a name (sesions), or an object you have not created yet in this session. Check spelling and capitals, and check you ran the line that creates it.

summarise_scores(sessions)

Error in `summarise_scores()`:
! could not find function "summarise_scores"


could not find function: a typo in a function name, or a package that is not loaded. Add the library() call.

"24" + 1

Error in `"24" + 1`:
! non-numeric argument to binary operator


non-numeric argument to binary operator: arithmetic on text. A number has been read or typed as character. Check with class().
read_csv("tidebreak_sessions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
Error: 'tidebreak_sessions.csv' does not exist in current working directory:
'C:/Users/you/L8-3DGD-Playtest-Analytics'.
does not exist or cannot open file: the path is wrong. Here the data/ folder is missing from it. Paths are relative to the project folder.
unexpected symbol, unexpected string constant or unexpected ')': a syntax error, almost always a missing comma, bracket or quote just before the point R names.
A warning is not an error. An error stops the code. A warning lets it finish but tells you something may be wrong, as as.numeric("twenty") did above. Never ignore a warning without reading it.

title: R from First Principles
text:
Worked Example
How many Build A sessions ended in frustration? This is the first number in Planning a Playtest. Here it is built from nothing, one idea at a time.
Load and look. Every analysis starts the same way:

sessions <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_sessions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(sessions |> select(build, quit_reason))

Rows: 120
Columns: 2
$ build       <chr> "A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B"…
$ quit_reason <chr> "Frustrated", "Lost interest", "Frustrated", "Lost interes…


One condition gives a logical vector, one value per session:

is_a <- sessions$build == "A"
sum(is_a)

[1] 60


Summing it counts the Build A sessions: 60.
Two conditions combine with &, “and”: TRUE only where both are true.

frustrated_a <- sessions$build == "A" & sessions$quit_reason == "Frustrated"
sum(frustrated_a)

[1] 20


20 sessions, out of 60.
Check it a second way. count() with two columns counts every combination at once:

sessions |> count(build, quit_reason)

# A tibble: 8 × 3
  build quit_reason         n
  <chr> <chr>           <int>
1 A     Completed test     31
2 A     Frustrated         20
3 A     Lost interest       7
4 A     Technical fault     2
5 B     Completed test     38
6 B     Frustrated          5
7 B     Lost interest      14
8 B     Technical fault     3


The A, Frustrated row says 20, the same answer. Getting a number two different ways is the cheapest check there is.
Nothing in this example is more than the ideas on this page: an object, a comparison, a logical vector, sum(), $, and one pipe.

title: R from First Principles
text:
Reading What R Tells You
[1] and friends are positions, not output. When a long vector wraps across lines, each line starts with the position of its first value: [1], then [19] and so on.
NA in a result means an unknown went in. Find it with is.na() before reaching for na.rm = TRUE.
A tibble prints its size and types first. # A tibble: 120 × 26 and the <chr>/<dbl> row under the names are the first check on any table.
Silence is success. Assignment prints nothing. If you want to see an object, type its name.
Red text is not always an error. Messages and warnings also print in red in most editors. Read the first word: Error stops the code, Warning does not.

title: R from First Principles
text:
Common Mistakes
Using = to compare. sessions$build = "A" is not a test. Comparison is ==.
Counting from 0. deaths[0] returns an empty vector, not the first value. R starts at 1.
Getting the case wrong. Sessions, sessions and SESSIONS are three different objects, and "Scout" does not equal "scout".
Forgetting the quotes, or adding them. "build" is the text build; build is an object called build. sum("deaths") is an error; sum(sessions$deaths) is a total.
Forgetting library(). Installed is not loaded. Every new session, and every Quarto document, needs its own library() calls.
Running lines out of order. The console remembers everything you have run in the session; a rendered document remembers only what is in it, from the top. If it works in the console and fails when rendered, something is missing from the document.
Naming an object after a function. mean <- 5 or data <- read_csv(...) works, but makes later code confusing. Pick names that describe the contents.
Leaving out na.rm = TRUE, or adding it without thinking. The first gives NA; the second silently drops data you may need to explain.

title: R from First Principles
text:
Practice
Each takes two or three minutes. Try each in the console before opening the answers.

Predict. What does each line return? c(1, 2, 3) * 2, sum(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)), c(5, 10, 15)[2], length(c("a", "b", NA)).
Fix it. Each line has one error. Find it without running the line first. mean(session$deaths), sum(sessions$build = "A"), Mean(sessions$deaths).
Compute. How many Tidebreak sessions lasted longer than 30 minutes, and what proportion is that?
Count. How many sessions came from each cohort?







NoteShow answers





1. Run them to check:

c(1, 2, 3) * 2

[1] 2 4 6

sum(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE))

[1] 2

c(5, 10, 15)[2]

[1] 10

length(c("a", "b", NA))

[1] 3


NA still occupies a position, so the last vector has length 3.
2. session should be sessions (object not found). = should be == (an error about an unexpected =). Mean should be mean: function names are case-sensitive too (could not find function).
3. A comparison, then sum() to count and mean() for the proportion:

sum(sessions$session_minutes > 30)

[1] 25

mean(sessions$session_minutes > 30)

[1] 0.2083333


25 sessions, or 21%.
4. One pipe:

sessions |> count(cohort)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  cohort      n
  <chr>   <int>
1 Novice     33
2 Regular    53
3 Veteran    34

title: R from First Principles
text:
Summary

R is a language built for data. Code records how you got an answer, so it can be checked and repeated; a spreadsheet records only the answer.
Try things in the console; keep them in a script or Quarto document; keep everything in a project.
<- creates an object. Every value has a type; R converts types silently, so check them.
The vector is R’s basic unit. Arithmetic is vectorised, and summing a logical vector counts it.
R counts from 1. A condition in square brackets keeps the elements where it is TRUE.
Arguments go by position or by name. Pass the main input by position and options by name. ?name opens the help.
NA means unknown and spreads through calculations. na.rm = TRUE leaves it out; is.na() finds it.
Read data with read_csv(), look at it with glimpse(), pull out a column with $.
The pipe |> reads “and then”. sessions |> count(build) counts sessions per build.
install.packages() once, library() every session. Read the error message before changing anything.








Key term
Meaning




Console
Where R runs code and prints results; nothing is kept


Script
A .R file of code you keep and re-run


Quarto document
A .qmd file of prose and code that renders to a web page


Project
The folder holding an analysis; paths are relative to it


Object
A named value, created with <-


Vector
An ordered set of values of one type


Index
A position or condition in [ ] that selects elements


Function
Code that takes arguments and returns a result


Argument
An input to a function, given by position or by name


NA
A missing value: unknown, not zero


Data frame
A table of equal-length column vectors; a tibble is one kind


Package
A bundle of extra functions, installed once and loaded with library()


Pipe
\|>: pass the result on the left into the function on the right

title: R from First Principles
text:
Reflective Questions

Think of an analysis you have done in a spreadsheet. What would a teammate need to repeat it exactly next week, and how much of that would be written down?
Vectorised arithmetic replaces most loops. Write, in C#, what sum(deaths > 2) does, and count the lines.
R converts types silently where C# would refuse to compile. Name one way that helps an analyst and one way it hurts.
A teammate’s Quarto report renders on their machine but not on yours. List three things that could cause it, from this page.

title: Start Here
text:
What You Are Learning
You are not training to be a statistician. You are learning to answer four questions about your own game, with evidence instead of opinion:








Question
What you do
Where you learn it




What happened?
Clean the data, describe it, look at it
Stage 1


Is the pattern credible?
Compare builds or groups; relate one measure to another
Stages 2 and 3


What does it mean for the game?
Interpret the result in terms of the player’s experience
every stage


What should we do next?
Recommend a change, a fix, or the next test
every stage, written up in Stage 4



The strip at the top of every notes page is the same idea as a process. Start with a question, decide what to measure, collect it, clean it, describe it, compare or relate, interpret, act. The highlighted steps are the ones that page covers.
Start with the question. Every technique in these notes is here because it answers a question a design team actually asks. If you cannot say what question a number answers, you do not need the number yet (rule 2).

How a Notes Page Works
Every notes page has the same shape, so you always know where to look.







Part
What it is for

Why a games team needs the idea at all

Not everything is core. Sections are marked when they are not:

No label: core. You need to understand this and be able to use it.

Exercise 03 — A missing value poisons the arithmetic [Do]
A seventh tester’s death count was not recorded. Add NA to the end of deaths and take the mean. Then take it again so that the result is a number.






NoteShow solution

mean(deaths)

[1] NA

NA is not zero and it is not “empty”. It means unknown, and the mean of a set containing an unknown value is itself unknown. R tells you that rather than quietly guessing.

Exercise 04 — Count with a condition [Apply]

deaths > 3

[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE  TRUE    NA

deaths[deaths > 3]

[1]  4  7  5 NA

[1] 3

mean(deaths > 3, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 0.5


Two things worth noticing. deaths[deaths > 3] keeps the NA, because R does not know whether the unknown value is above 3 or not. And sum() on a TRUE/FALSE vector counts the TRUEs, because TRUE is 1 and FALSE is 0, so mean() gives the proportion.

title: Lab 01 — Reading Data
text:
Exercise 09 — “Only one in five” [Decide]
The producer counts the quit reasons and says: “Only one in five players quit in frustration. Most players are fine, so frustration is not a priority.” Count quit_reason, then find the share of frustration quits in each build, and decide whether the producer’s reading is defensible.






NoteShow solution






sessions |> count(quit_reason)

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  quit_reason         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 Completed test     69
2 Frustrated         25
3 Lost interest      21
4 Technical fault     5

sessions |>
  group_by(build) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            frustrated = mean(quit_reason == "Frustrated"))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  build     n frustrated
  <chr> <int>      <dbl>
1 A        60     0.333 
2 B        60     0.0833


One defensible answer: no, because “one in five” averages two different games. Overall, 25 of 120 sessions ended in frustration, 21%. Split by build, that is 20 of 60 in Build A (33%) and 5 of 60 in Build B (8%). One build loses a third of its players to frustration; the other hardly any. The overall figure describes neither.
What makes it defensible. It breaks the count down by the one thing the playtest was designed to compare before judging it, and it reads the numbers as a difference between builds rather than a verdict on the game.
What would make it indefensible. Accepting “one in five” because it is smaller than the number who completed the test, without asking where the one in five came from. Or going the other way and calling the whole game frustrating, when Build B barely is.



Write 2 sentences: what would you say to the producer instead, and what would you want to check next?

title: Lab 01 — Reading Data
section: Exercise 10 — Describe a numeric variable properly [Apply]
text:
Exercise 10 — Describe a numeric variable properly [Apply]
For score and for session_minutes, compute the mean, median, standard deviation, quartiles and IQR.






NoteShow solution






mean(sessions$score)

[1] 1428.767

median(sessions$score)

[1] 1470

sd(sessions$score)

[1] 319.2236

quantile(sessions$score)

     0%     25%     50%     75%    100% 
 541.00 1270.00 1470.00 1628.75 2019.00 

IQR(sessions$score)

[1] 358.75

sessions |>
  summarise(mean   = mean(session_minutes),
            median = median(session_minutes),
            sd     = sd(session_minutes),
            iqr    = IQR(session_minutes))

# A tibble: 1 × 4
   mean median    sd   iqr
  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1  22.8   26.2  7.76  13.8


Both ways work. The first is quick for one variable; summarise() puts every summary in one table, which is what you want once there is more than one. quantile() with no second argument gives the five-number summary.



Write 2 sentences: express the gap between mean and median as a percentage of the median, for both variables. Which one is more skewed, and does its tail run left or right?






NoteShow answer





Score’s mean sits 2.8% below its median. Session minutes sits 12.9% below. Both are left-skewed: the mean falls below the median because a group of low values drags it down. But session minutes is far more so.
Comparing the raw gaps (-41 points against -3.4 minutes) would have told you the opposite, which is why the scale of the variable always has to come into it.

title: Lab 01 — Reading Data
section: Exercise 14 — When do we lose them? [Decide]
text:
Exercise 14 — When do we lose them? [Decide]
The producer has the two mean session lengths, 21.3 minutes for Build A and 24.2 for Build B, and says: “Build A sessions are about three minutes shorter. Players drift off a bit sooner, that’s all.”
A retention curve shows the share of sessions still going at every minute. Run this code to draw one for each build; you do not need to be able to write it. Then decide whether “drift off a bit sooner” is a fair description.

mins_a <- sessions$session_minutes[sessions$build == "A"]
mins_b <- sessions$session_minutes[sessions$build == "B"]

minute  <- 0:32
still_a <- sapply(minute, function(m) mean(mins_a >= m))
still_b <- sapply(minute, function(m) mean(mins_b >= m))

plot(minute, still_a, type = "s", lwd = 2, col = "grey40", ylim = c(0, 1),
     main = "Share of sessions still playing",
     xlab = "Minute", ylab = "Share still playing")
lines(minute, still_b, type = "s", lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
legend("bottomleft", legend = c("Build A", "Build B"), lwd = 2,
       col = c("grey40", "firebrick"), bty = "n")








mean(mins_a >= m) is the share of Build A sessions that lasted at least m minutes, the proportion trick again; sapply() repeats it for every minute.






NoteShow solution





One defensible answer: no. Build A does not drift; it drops. Between minutes 11 and 13, Build A loses 20% of its sessions; Build B loses 7% over the same two minutes. Something in the first dozen minutes of Build A drives a block of players out at once, and Exercise 09 already showed those quits are frustration. The investigation should start at minute 11 of Build A: watch the replays, check where those players were.
What makes it defensible. It looks at when players left, not just the average, and names a specific moment someone can investigate.
What would make it indefensible. Comparing the two means, agreeing that the difference is “a bit”, and moving on. The mean folds a sharp exit at minute 12 and a long tail of full sessions into one number that describes neither (rule 9).



Write 2 sentences: what would you ask the level designer to check first, and what number would tell you, in the next playtest, that the fix worked?

text:
Exercise 05 — Write the cleaning log [Decide]
Decide what to do with the rows that have gaps, then write the cleaning log for clean: every step, the number of rows after it, and why. Your log is the record a reader of the report would use to check your n (rule 6).
Before you decide, compare each build’s median session_minutes with the blanks left out, against the median of the Build A frustration quits that were recorded.






NoteShow solution






clean |>
  group_by(build) |>
  summarise(median_minutes = median(session_minutes, na.rm = TRUE),
            missing        = sum(is.na(session_minutes)))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  build median_minutes missing
  <chr>          <dbl>   <int>
1 A               26.2       8
2 B               27.1       0

clean |>
  filter(build == "A", quit_reason == "Frustrated") |>
  summarise(recorded = sum(!is.na(session_minutes)),
            median_minutes = median(session_minutes, na.rm = TRUE))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  recorded median_minutes
     <int>          <dbl>
1       12           11.2

sum(complete.cases(clean))   # what "drop every incomplete row" would leave

[1] 109


One defensible answer: keep every row, and handle the gaps per analysis.








Step
Rows after
Why




Raw export
124
As delivered


Remove exact duplicates
120
4 sessions exported twice; no key duplicates with different values


Standardise cohort
120
18 labels had stray spaces or inconsistent capitals


Keep blank session_minutes
120
All 8 are Build A frustration quits. Summaries of session length exclude them and say so


Keep blank deaths
120
3 rows, no pattern. Excluded from deaths summaries only



What makes it defensible. The blank session lengths are not random. Recorded Build A frustration quits have a median of 11.2 minutes, so the missing ones are almost certainly short, and Build A’s median of 26.1 minutes is an overestimate. Keeping the rows keeps their quit_reason, which is complete and carries the finding. The log says what every summary of session length is missing, so a reader can judge it.
What would make it indefensible. Dropping every incomplete row by reflex, which silently takes n from 120 to 109 and removes the frustration quits the comparison is about. Or filling the blanks with 0 or with Build A’s average, which invents session lengths and hides the logging fault.



Write 3 sentences: the blank session lengths are also a bug in Build A’s telemetry. Who should hear about it, and what goes in the bug report?






ImportantBefore Part B



Part B uses sessions from the Setup block, not your clean. It is the same sessions, exported again after the logging fault was fixed: the same rows, with the gaps you found filled.

identical(clean$session_id, sessions$session_id)

[1] TRUE

[1] 0

[1] 0


Everything Part B compares is therefore free of the bias you found in Exercise 05. In a real playtest you would rarely get that second export. Your cleaning log is what you would have instead.

title: Lab 02 — Comparing Builds
section: Exercise 08 — Could it be chance? Read the shuffle [Do]
text:
Exercise 08 — Could it be chance? Read the shuffle [Do]
If the signposting made no difference, the build label on each session would be arbitrary. This code shuffles the labels 10,000 times, recomputes the gap in mean wrong turns each time, and counts how many shuffled gaps are at least as large as the real one. You do not need to be able to write it. Run it, and compare the result with Exercise 07’s p-value.

gap <- function(y, g) mean(y[g == "A"]) - mean(y[g == "B"])

observed <- gap(sessions$wrong_turns, sessions$build)
set.seed(1)
shuffled <- replicate(10000, gap(sessions$wrong_turns, sample(sessions$build)))

observed

[1] 3.4

max(abs(shuffled))

[1] 2.166667

mean(abs(shuffled) >= abs(observed))   # the shuffle's p-value

[1] 0

hist(shuffled, breaks = 40, col = "grey85", border = "white",
     xlim = range(c(shuffled, observed)),
     main = "Gaps from shuffled build labels",
     xlab = "Difference in mean wrong turns (A - B)")
abline(v = observed, col = "firebrick", lwd = 3)














NoteShow solution





The real gap is 3.4 wrong turns; the largest of ten thousand shuffled gaps is 2.17. No shuffle came close, so the shuffle’s p-value is below 1 in 10,000, which agrees with the t-test’s tiny p-value. The shuffle shows what a p-value is: the share of a world without a difference that looks at least as extreme as your data.



Write 2 sentences: what does one shuffle represent, and why does the proportion of extreme shuffles answer “could this be chance?”

section: Exercise 09 — The same players, both builds [Apply]
text:
Exercise 09 — The same players, both builds [Apply]
paired records 30 players who each played both builds. Run the paired t-test on wrong_turns_a and wrong_turns_b, then run the unpaired test on the same two columns. Compare the widths of the two confidence intervals.






NoteShow solution






paired_test   <- t.test(paired$wrong_turns_a, paired$wrong_turns_b, paired = TRUE)
unpaired_test <- t.test(paired$wrong_turns_a, paired$wrong_turns_b)

paired_test$conf.int

[1] 1.838014 3.695319
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

unpaired_test$conf.int

[1] 1.180570 4.352763
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

diff(paired_test$conf.int)

[1] 1.857305

diff(unpaired_test$conf.int)

[1] 3.172193


Same estimate, but the paired interval is 1.9 wrong turns wide against 3.2. The paired test compares each player with themselves, so differences in player skill cancel out. diff() of an interval is its width.



Write 2 sentences: the paired file does not record which build each player played first. Why does that matter, and what would you change about the next paired study?

title: Lab 02 — Comparing Builds
section: Exercise 10 — No difference, or cannot tell? [Apply]
text:
Exercise 10 — No difference, or cannot tell? [Apply]
Run the t-test on enjoyment by build and on items_collected by build. Neither is significant. For which one can you say there is no meaningful difference, and for which can you only say we cannot tell?






NoteShow solution






enjoy <- t.test(enjoyment ~ build, data = sessions)
items <- t.test(items_collected ~ build, data = sessions)

enjoy$conf.int

[1] -0.3483742  0.3483742
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

items$conf.int

[1] -1.0061446  0.3394779
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

sessions |> summarise(mean_items = mean(items_collected))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_items
       <dbl>
1       4.18


Read each interval against the size of the variable. Enjoyment’s interval runs from -0.35 to 0.35 on a seven-point scale: whatever the true difference is, it is too small to matter. That is no meaningful difference. The items interval runs from -1.01 to 0.34 items, when a typical player collects about 4. Build B’s players could be collecting up to 1.0 more items each, or up to 0.3 fewer. That is cannot tell.
“Cannot tell” means this playtest was too small to see a difference of that size. A bigger playtest, or a paired one, would narrow the interval enough to decide (Testing in Depth).



Write 2 sentences: why is “not significant” a weaker statement than “the confidence interval is narrow and sits around zero”?

title: Lab 02 — Comparing Builds
section: Exercise 11 — “Players play longer in Build B” [Decide]
text:
Exercise 11 — “Players play longer in Build B” [Decide]
t.test(session_minutes ~ build) gives p = 0.037, and Build B’s sessions are about 3 minutes longer on average. The producer wants to put “players play 3 minutes longer in Build B” in the pitch. Do you let them? Test before you decide: compare session length between the builds for players who did not quit in frustration.






NoteShow solution






not_frustrated <- sessions |> filter(quit_reason != "Frustrated")
t.test(session_minutes ~ build, data = not_frustrated)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  session_minutes by build
t = 0.63783, df = 88.126, p-value = 0.5252
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group A and group B is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -1.564143  3.042780
sample estimates:
mean in group A mean in group B 
       26.19750        25.45818 

sessions |>
  filter(quit_reason == "Frustrated") |>
  group_by(build) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median_minutes = median(session_minutes))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  build     n median_minutes
  <chr> <int>          <dbl>
1 A        20           11.7
2 B         5           11.7


One defensible answer: no, because the claim describes the wrong thing. Among players who did not quit in frustration, Build A averaged 26.2 minutes and Build B 25.5 (p = 0.53). Frustration quits end at a median of about 11.7 minutes in both builds. Build B does not make anyone play longer. It makes fewer people quit early, and that pulls its average up. The honest pitch line is “fewer players quit in frustration”, which is also the stronger claim.
What makes it defensible. It checks what is driving the difference before describing it, and it replaces the claim with one the data supports.
What would make it indefensible. Approving the line because the p-value is below 0.05. The difference is real; the explanation attached to it is not.



Write 3 sentences: a significant difference in a mean can come from every player shifting a little or from a few players shifting a lot. How do you tell which, and why does it change the design conclusion?

title: Lab 02 — Comparing Builds
section: Exercise 12 — Which number goes in the report? [Decide]
text:
Exercise 12 — Which number goes in the report? [Decide]
You have three estimates of how much the signposting reduced wrong turns: the session-level test from Exercise 07, the paired study from Exercise 09, and a player-level test that averages each player’s 4 sessions first. Run the player-level test, then decide which result leads the report.






NoteShow solution






per_player <- sessions |>
  group_by(player_id, build) |>
  summarise(wrong_turns = mean(wrong_turns), .groups = "drop")
player_test <- t.test(wrong_turns ~ build, data = per_player)

player_test$conf.int

[1] 2.361153 4.438847
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

result$conf.int

[1] 2.480141 4.319859
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

paired_test$conf.int

[1] 1.838014 3.695319
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95


One defensible answer: lead with the player-level result, and cite the paired study as support. The session-level test treats 120 sessions as independent when they come from 30 players, so its interval is narrower than the data justifies. The player-level interval, 2.4 to 4.4 wrong turns, is honest about that. The paired study, a different design with different players, points the same way, which is worth more than any single p-value.
What makes it defensible. It picks the analysis whose assumptions match how the data was collected, and it uses the other two as corroboration rather than choosing between them.
What would make it indefensible. Picking whichever result has the smallest p-value or the largest effect. That is choosing the answer, not the analysis.



Write 2 sentences: why is agreement between two differently designed studies stronger evidence than a very small p-value from one?

Exercise 03 — The navigation figure [Apply]
Build a report figure for the navigation result: the distribution of wrong_turns in each build, in panels stacked so the x axes line up, labelled for a level designer.

ggplot(sessions, aes(x = wrong_turns)) +

title: Lab 03 — A Figure for Your Report
text:
Exercise 04 — Fix this figure [Apply]
A teammate made this figure for the report to show how sessions ended in each build. Find three things wrong with it, then fix them.

ggplot(sessions, aes(x = quit_reason)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = "grey")) +
  labs(x = "quit_reason")














NoteShow solution






ggplot(sessions, aes(y = quit_reason)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "grey60") +
  facet_wrap(~ build) +
  labs(title = "How sessions ended, by build",
       x = "Sessions", y = NULL)








Three problems, three fixes:

It does not split by build, so it cannot answer the question it is for. facet_wrap(~ build) puts the builds side by side.
fill = "grey" is inside aes(), so ggplot2 treats “grey” as data: the bars come out in a default colour, with a meaningless legend. A fixed colour goes outside aes().
The labels are for R, not for a reader. There is no title and the axis says quit_reason. y = NULL removes a label that would only repeat the category names, and putting the categories on y makes the long names readable.




Write 1 sentence: which of the three problems would most mislead a producer who glanced at the figure for five seconds?

title: Lab 03 — A Figure for Your Report
text:
Exercise 05 — Which figure leads? [Decide]
The report has room for one figure about enjoyment. Draw two candidates: a boxplot of enjoyment by build, and a bar chart of enjoyment faceted by build. Decide which one goes in the report.






NoteShow solution






ggplot(sessions, aes(x = build, y = enjoyment)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey85") +
  labs(title = "Enjoyment by build", x = "Build", y = "Enjoyment (1-7)")









ggplot(sessions, aes(x = enjoyment)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "grey60") +
  facet_wrap(~ build, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Enjoyment rating, by build", x = "Enjoyment (1-7)", y = "Sessions")








One defensible answer: the faceted bar chart. Enjoyment is a 1–7 rating, so it has only seven possible values. The bars show exactly how many players chose each one, and the two builds’ shapes can be compared directly. The boxplot reduces a seven-value rating to five numbers, several of which land on the same value, and looks more precise than the data is.
What makes it defensible. It matches the geometry to the variable type (rule 3) and to the comparison the reader is meant to make.
What would make it indefensible. Choosing the boxplot because it looks more “statistical”, or putting both in the report so the reader has to work out which one matters.

title: Testing in Depth
text: Going further. This page extends Comparing Groups. Nothing here is needed for the labs or the assessment. Read it when you are planning how many players a playtest needs, when you are tempted to test every survey item, or when the mean is the wrong thing to compare.

title: Testing in Depth
text:
Two Ways to Be Wrong
A test makes a decision from incomplete information, so it can be wrong in two directions.









The build really makes no difference
The build really makes a difference




Test says “significant”
Type I error: a false alarm
Correct


Test says “not significant”
Correct
Type II error: a missed effect



A Type I error is acting on a difference that is not there: rebuilding a level because of a fluke. Its rate is α. To check, draw two groups of 30 from the same population of wrong turns, so there is no real difference, and test them two thousand times: 5.3% come out significant, close to the 5% that α = 0.05 promises.
A Type II error is missing a difference that is there: shipping a build with a problem because the playtest was too small to see it. The chance of avoiding it is the test’s power. Power grows with sample size. Drawing playtests of different sizes from Tidebreak’s real Build A and Build B sessions, and counting how often the t-test detects the signposting effect:



Sessions per build
5
10
15
30




Chance of detecting the effect
44%
78%
94%
>99%



Even this large effect is missed more often than not with five sessions per build. A smaller effect needs far more players. Plan the playtest size around the smallest difference that would change your decision, which is the “how many players” question from Planning a Playtest, now with numbers.
The two errors trade off. A stricter α, such as 0.01, means fewer false alarms and more missed effects. Which mistake is worse depends on the decision: a false alarm that costs a week of rework, or a missed problem that ships to every player.






NoteThe simulation code






# Type I: two samples from the same population, tested 2,000 times
pop_wt <- rep(sessions$wrong_turns, times = 1000)
mean(replicate(2000, t.test(sample(pop_wt, 30), sample(pop_wt, 30))$p.value < 0.05))

# Power: samples of n from each real build, tested 2,000 times
power_at <- function(n) {
  mean(replicate(2000, t.test(sample(wt_a, n, TRUE), sample(wt_b, n, TRUE))$p.value < 0.05))
}
sapply(c(5, 10, 15, 30), power_at)

title: Testing in Depth
text:
Testing Many Things at Once
At α = 0.05, each test on a difference that is not real has a 5% chance of a false alarm. Run several and the chances add up. With eight independent tests, the chance that at least one comes up significant by luck alone is 1 − 0.95^8 = 34%.
The Tidebreak survey has 8 items. Testing each one by build:

sv <- merge(survey, sessions[, c("session_id", "build")])
round(sort(sapply(names(survey)[-1],
                  function(i) t.test(sv[[i]] ~ sv$build)$p.value)), 3)

    objective_clear controls_responsive    death_understood        match_length 
              0.000               0.150               0.257               0.273 
    difficulty_fair     level_navigable        visual_style    would_play_again 
              0.724               0.854               0.884               1.000 


One item, objective_clear, is significant. Is it real, or the one-in-three false alarm? Three things say real. It survives the simplest correction, Bonferroni: divide α by the number of tests, here 0.05 / 8 = 0.0063, and its p-value is still below that. It was the item the team expected to move, written down before the test. And it agrees with the telemetry: Build A had the frustration quits.
The defence is to decide in advance. Name the comparisons that answer your question before you run any of them. A result you went looking for after scanning twenty tests needs a second playtest before anyone acts on it (rule 1).

title: Testing in Depth
text:
Q-Q Plots and the t-Test
A t-test assumes the means are roughly normal. With a few dozen players per group that is nearly always true, thanks to the central limit theorem (Sampling Theory). A Q-Q plot is the standard visual check on the data itself. Close to the line means close to normal:

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
qqnorm(sessions$wrong_turns, main = "Wrong turns", pch = 19, cex = 0.6,
       col = pal$line)
qqline(sessions$wrong_turns, col = pal$highlight, lwd = 2)
b_ms <- frames$ms[frames$build == "B"]
qqnorm(b_ms, main = "Build B frame times", pch = 19, cex = 0.4, col = pal$line)
qqline(b_ms, col = pal$highlight, lwd = 2)
par(op)







Figure 1: Wrong turns (left) follow the line in steps, because they are whole numbers: fine for a t-test. Build B’s frame times (right) bend sharply away at the top: a long tail the mean cannot describe.





Strong outliers and a mismatched design matter far more than normality, and no amount of data fixes the wrong design.

title: Testing in Depth
text:
A Shuffle for Any Summary
The permutation test on the notes page shuffled the build labels and recomputed a difference in means. Nothing about the shuffle needs a mean. Replace it with any summary that answers your question, and the logic is unchanged. That makes it the fallback when the mean is the wrong thing to compare.
Frame times are the case. The question is not “is Build B’s average frame slower?” but “is Build B’s worst one per cent slower?”. In the Corridor:

corr <- frames[frames$zone == "Corridor", ]

p99_gap <- function(ms, g) quantile(ms[g == "B"], 0.99) - quantile(ms[g == "A"], 0.99)

observed <- p99_gap(corr$ms, corr$build)
set.seed(9)
shuffled <- replicate(2000, p99_gap(corr$ms, sample(corr$build)))

observed

    99% 
29.1245 

mean(abs(shuffled) >= abs(observed))

[1] 0


Build B’s 99th percentile in the Corridor is 29.1 ms slower than Build A’s, and none of 2,000 shuffles produced a gap that large: the hitch is not chance. A t-test on the same frames would answer a different question, about the mean, which is the one that hides the hitch.

title: Reshaping and Joining
text: Going further. This page extends Interpreting and Reporting Evidence. You need it when your data arrives in more than one file, or in a shape that does not suit the question. Nothing here is required for the labs.

title: Reshaping and Joining
Reshaping and Joining
text:
Joins
A join adds columns from one table to another by matching on a key, a column both tables share, such as session_id.








Join
Keeps
Use when




left_join(x, y)
Every row of x, with y’s columns where there is a match, NA where not
Adding information to your main table. The usual choice


inner_join(x, y)
Only rows with a match in both
You only want sessions that have both a log and a survey


anti_join(x, y)
Rows of x with no match in y
Finding what is missing: sessions with no survey




nrow(sessions)

[1] 120

nrow(survey)

[1] 120

sessions |> left_join(survey, by = "session_id") |> nrow()

[1] 120

sessions |> anti_join(survey, by = "session_id") |> nrow()

[1] 0


Every session has a survey here, so the join keeps all 120 rows and the anti-join finds none. Real exports are rarely that tidy.

Checking a join
Run these three checks every time you join:

Did the row count change? A left_join() should keep the rows of x. If it gains rows, the key is repeated in y.
Are there new NAs? Rows of x with no match get NA in every new column. Count them, and find them with anti_join().
Is the key really unique? count(key) |> filter(n > 1) on each table.


survey |> count(session_id) |> filter(n > 1)   # no repeated keys: good

# A tibble: 0 × 2
# ℹ 2 variables: session_id <chr>, n <int>

joined <- sessions |> left_join(survey, by = "session_id")
sum(is.na(joined$objective_clear))             # no unmatched sessions: good

[1] 0


A join that silently duplicates rows is one of the commonest ways for a playtest analysis to go wrong without an error. Two survey rows for one session double that session in every summary. The checks take a minute.

title: Is It Normal Enough?
text: Going further. This page extends Distributions and Shape. Nothing here is needed for the labs or the assessment. Read it if you want to know how to check a shape properly, or when a later page or a paper you are reading assumes data is “approximately normal”.

title: Is It Normal Enough?
text:
z-scores
A z-score says how many standard deviations a value sits from the mean:
\[z = \frac{\text{value} - \text{mean}}{\text{SD}}\]
A player with an awareness rating of 90 has \(z = (90 - 66.2) / 12.4 = 1.9\): nearly 2 SDs above average. If awareness is normal-shaped, the 68–95–99.7 rule puts that in roughly the top few per cent.
z-scores let you compare values measured on different scales: “two SDs above average” means the same thing for a score, a time or a rating.
The catch is the “if”. For a skewed variable the SD is inflated by the tail, and the rule no longer tells you how unusual a value is. Score is a good example:

(2000 - mean(sessions$score)) / sd(sessions$score)

[1] 1.789446

mean(sessions$score < 2000)

[1] 0.9916667


A score of 2,000 is about 1.8 SDs above the mean. But the Sentinel collapses give score a left tail, which inflates the SD and drags the mean down. The percentile is more honest: 99% of sessions scored below 2,000.

title: Is It Normal Enough?
text:
Checking the Bell Shape
Real data is never exactly normal. The useful question is whether it is close enough for the 68–95–99.7 rule to work. Draw the histogram on a density scale and lay the normal curve with the same mean and SD over it:

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 3, 2, 1))
hist(aw, breaks = 12, freq = FALSE, col = pal$fill, border = "white",
     main = "Awareness", xlab = "Rating", ylab = "")
curve(dnorm(x, mean(aw), sd(aw)), add = TRUE, lwd = 2, col = pal$highlight)
hist(sm, breaks = 12, freq = FALSE, col = pal$fill, border = "white",
     main = "Session length", xlab = "Minutes", ylab = "")
curve(dnorm(x, mean(sm), sd(sm)), add = TRUE, lwd = 2, col = pal$highlight)
par(op)







Figure 1: Awareness follows the normal curve closely; session length, piled up against its 32-minute cap, does not.





freq = FALSE draws the histogram as a density, so the bars and the curve share a scale. curve() draws a function of x; dnorm() is the normal curve.
The rule makes a checkable prediction, so check it. abs(x - mean(x)) < k * sd(x) is TRUE for every value within k SDs of the mean, and its mean() is the proportion:

within_sd <- function(x, k) mean(abs(x - mean(x)) < k * sd(x))
within_sd(sessions$awareness, 1)

[1] 0.65

within_sd(sessions$session_minutes, 1)

[1] 0.575





Variable
Within 1 SD
Within 2 SDs
Verdict




Normal distribution
68%
95%



awareness
65%
98%
close: the rule works


distance_m
61%
98%
symmetric but flatter than a bell


session_minutes
57%
100%
not normal: skewed and capped


Build B frame ms
98%
99%
not normal: a spike and a long tail



For session length, “mean ± 1 SD” covers only 57% of sessions, so quoting the mean and SD as if they described a bell would mislead. For frame times, the SD is inflated by a handful of very slow frames, and the mean ± 2 SDs covers almost every frame while saying nothing about the ones that matter.

title: Is It Normal Enough?
text:
Q-Q Plots
A Q-Q plot is a sharper check than a histogram. It plots each value against where it would fall if the data were perfectly normal. Normal data lies along a straight line; skew bends the ends away from it.

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
qqnorm(aw, main = "Awareness", pch = 19, cex = 0.6); qqline(aw, col = pal$highlight)
qqnorm(sm, main = "Session length", pch = 19, cex = 0.6); qqline(sm, col = pal$highlight)
par(op)







Figure 2: Awareness hugs the line; session length flattens out at the top, where values pile up against the 32-minute cap.





You will see Q-Q plots in discussions of the assumptions behind a t-test.

title: Is It Normal Enough?
text:
Why It Matters Later
Even when individual values are far from normal, the averages of samples tend to be close to normal. That fact, the central limit theorem, is what makes confidence intervals and t-tests work on data like session length. It is why the Stage 2 notes can use a t-test on skewed playtest data, as long as the sample is not tiny and there is no extreme tail. For the Stage 2 version, see From Sample to Population.
Formal normality tests (Shapiro–Wilk and others) exist, and you will see them in papers. They are not used in this course. With small samples they rarely detect anything; with large ones they flag differences too small to matter. The histogram and the Q-Q plot tell you more.

title: Is It Normal Enough?
text:
Try It
Check the 68–95 rule against kills and distance_m, then draw a Q-Q plot of each. Which one would you describe with a mean and SD, and which with a median and IQR?






NoteShow answer






within_sd(sessions$kills, 1)

[1] 0.775

within_sd(sessions$distance_m, 1)

[1] 0.6083333

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
qqnorm(sessions$kills, main = "Kills", pch = 19, cex = 0.6)
qqline(sessions$kills, col = pal$highlight)
qqnorm(sessions$distance_m, main = "Distance", pch = 19, cex = 0.6)
qqline(sessions$distance_m, col = pal$highlight)







par(op)

Neither matches the rule exactly. kills puts 78% within 1 SD: it is a small count, so its values bunch on a few whole numbers and its Q-Q plot is a staircase. distance_m puts 61% there: symmetric, but flatter than a bell, so the points follow the line in the middle and bend at the ends.
Distance is the one to describe with a mean and SD: it is symmetric, its mean and median almost coincide, and the SD is a fair guide to spread. For kills, report the median and IQR, or simply the count at each value: with so few possible values, the counts are the clearest description.

title: Stage 3 Demo
section: Demo 1 — A figure, one layer at a time (3A)
text:
Demo 1 — A figure, one layer at a time (3A)
Step 1. Data and mapping, no geometry

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

sessions <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_sessions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Data plus mapping gives axes and nothing else: no geometry, no marks.
ggplot(sessions, aes(x = wrong_turns))








Step 2. Add a geometry

# + adds a layer. binwidth = 1 because wrong turns are whole numbers.
ggplot(sessions, aes(x = wrong_turns)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1)








Question. This is correct. Why does it not answer “did Build B help”?
Step 3. Map a group, and watch it mislead

# fill = build inside aes() is a MAPPING: colour follows the data, legend appears.
# But histograms stack by default, so Build A floats on top of Build B.
ggplot(sessions, aes(x = wrong_turns, fill = build)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1)








Step 4. Facet instead, and label it for a reader

# One panel per build, stacked so the x axes line up.
# fill = "grey60" OUTSIDE aes() is SETTING: fixed colour, no legend needed.
ggplot(sessions, aes(x = wrong_turns)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "grey60", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ build, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Wrong turns per session, by build",
       x = "Wrong turns", y = "Sessions")








Question. Build B is lower. What else is different about its shape? What caption would you write under this in the report?
Step 5. The mapping bug, on purpose

# "blue" inside aes() is treated as data: salmon points, and a legend saying "blue".
ggplot(sessions, aes(x = awareness, y = score)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = "blue"))








Move colour = "blue" outside aes() live, then open your own data. That is the rest of the clinic.

title: Stage 3 Demo
section: Demo 2 — Relationships, and when to distrust them (3B)
text:
Demo 2 — Relationships, and when to distrust them (3B)
Step 6. The scatterplot, then the number

# colour SET outside aes(); geom_smooth(method = "lm") adds a straight-line trend.
ggplot(sessions, aes(x = awareness, y = score)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey40") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black") +
  labs(title = "Awareness against score", x = "Awareness rating", y = "Score")







cor(sessions$awareness, sessions$score)    # the picture, as one number

[1] 0.5907852

cor(sessions$shots_fired, sessions$score)  # the stat everyone assumes matters

[1] 0.05307857


Question. So should we buff awareness? Hold the answer until Step 9.
Step 7. Many at once: the correlation matrix

# Spearman, because difficulty and enjoyment are 1-7 ratings.
sessions |>
  select(deaths, wrong_turns, difficulty, enjoyment, session_minutes) |>
  cor(method = "spearman") |>
  round(2)

                deaths wrong_turns difficulty enjoyment session_minutes
deaths            1.00       -0.03       0.57     -0.20           -0.02
wrong_turns      -0.03        1.00      -0.09     -0.03            0.04
difficulty        0.57       -0.09       1.00     -0.33            0.15
enjoyment        -0.20       -0.03      -0.33      1.00            0.23
session_minutes  -0.02        0.04       0.15      0.23            1.00


Question. Read the deaths row. Which pair goes together most? Which measure goes with nothing at all?
Step 8. Telemetry against self-report

survey <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_survey.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

joined <- sessions |> left_join(survey, by = "session_id")

# Did players who got lost rate the level as harder to navigate?
cor(joined$wrong_turns, joined$level_navigable, method = "spearman")

[1] 0.05151128

joined |>
  group_by(build) |>
  summarise(wrong_turns = mean(wrong_turns), navigable = mean(level_navigable))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  build wrong_turns navigable
  <chr>       <dbl>     <dbl>
1 A            8.92      3.2 
2 B            5.52      3.23


Question. Build A’s players got lost far more, and rated navigation the same. What does that say about asking players whether they got lost?
Step 9. A strong correlation that means the opposite

cor(sessions$mobility, sessions$survivability)   # faster players are more fragile?

[1] -0.6562375

# Map colour to archetype: one cloud and one trend line per group.
ggplot(sessions, aes(x = mobility, y = survivability, colour = archetype)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Mobility rating", y = "Survivability rating", colour = "Archetype")







sessions |>
  group_by(archetype) |>
  summarise(r = cor(mobility, survivability))     # the same, within each group

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  archetype     r
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 Duelist   0.302
2 Engineer  0.512
3 Scout     0.465
4 Sentinel  0.598


Question. The overall correlation is negative; every archetype’s line goes up. Which one answers “should a Scout lose health as they get faster”? Archetype is the confounder. Back to Step 6: what would you need to do before buffing awareness? (A test, not a patch.) This is Lab 04, Exercise 06; then open your own data.

NoteGet the files




Demo code: stage-0-demo.qmd, every chunk on this page in one file you can run.
Data: none to download. The demo types its invented survey in; Step 1 shows how to load your own class’s CSV instead.
The data is a four-question class survey: height, MBTI personality type, favourite game genre and preferred drink. class |> count(type, sort = TRUE)

   type n
1  INFP 4
2  INTP 3
3  INFJ 2
4  INTJ 2
5  ISTP 2
6  ENFP 1
7  ENTJ 1
8  ENTP 1
9  ESFJ 1
10 ESTP 1
11 ISFJ 1
12 ISFP 1

class |> count(beverage)

  beverage  n
1   Coffee 10
2  Neither  3
3      Tea  7


substr(x, 1, 4) keeps characters 1 to 4. if_else(test, yes, no) gives yes where the test is TRUE and no where it is not, so only the typo changes.
Question. What goes in the cleaning log? (Two lines: INFP-Mediator recoded, Cofee recoded. No rows removed, but two students changed group.)
Step 4. A value that cannot be right

class |>
  summarise(min = min(height, na.rm = TRUE),
            max = max(height, na.rm = TRUE))

   min max
1 1.78 186

class |> filter(height < 100)   # nobody is under a metre tall

  id height       mbti_type                genre beverage type
1 15   1.78 ISTP - Virtuoso First-Person Shooter   Coffee ISTP


One student is 1.78 cm tall. Nobody is. They answered in metres, not centimetres, so the fix is to multiply by 100:

class <- class |>
  mutate(height = if_else(height < 3, height * 100, height))

class |> summarise(min = min(height, na.rm = TRUE),
                   max = max(height, na.rm = TRUE))

  min max
1 148 186


Question. Why fix 1.78 but keep 148? (1.78 is impossible and the meaning is clear: 178 cm. 148 cm is unusual but possible.)
Step 5. New columns from old ones

# Each letter of the type is one dimension. With this few students, the 16 types
# are too thin to compare, but each letter splits the class in two.
class <- class |>
  mutate(mind   = if_else(substr(type, 1, 1) == "E", "Extravert", "Introvert"),
         nature = if_else(substr(type, 3, 3) == "T", "Thinking", "Feeling"))

class |> count(mind)

       mind  n
1 Extravert  5
2 Introvert 15

class |> count(nature)

    nature  n
1  Feeling 10
2 Thinking 10


Step 6. Describe one number: height

class |>
  summarise(answered = sum(!is.na(height)),   # how many heights we actually have
            mean     = mean(height, na.rm = TRUE),
            median   = median(height, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd       = sd(height, na.rm = TRUE),
            iqr      = IQR(height, na.rm = TRUE),
            min      = min(height, na.rm = TRUE),
            max      = max(height, na.rm = TRUE))

  answered     mean median       sd iqr min max
1       19 172.4211    174 9.154937  10 148 186



hist(class$height, breaks = seq(140, 200, by = 5),
     col = "grey85", border = "white",
     main = "Height of the class", xlab = "Height (cm)", ylab = "Students")
abline(v = median(class$height, na.rm = TRUE), lty = 2, lwd = 2)        # median
abline(v = mean(class$height, na.rm = TRUE), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2) # mean
legend("topleft", legend = c("median", "mean"), lty = c(2, 1),
       col = c("black", "firebrick"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")








Question. Why answered, not n()? Which way did 148 cm pull the mean? (One row has no height. Down: the mean is below the median.)
Step 7. Describe a category: counts and proportions

drinks <- class |>
  count(beverage, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(prop = round(n / sum(n), 2))   # each count as a share of the class
drinks

  beverage  n prop
1   Coffee 10 0.50
2      Tea  7 0.35
3  Neither  3 0.15



barplot(drinks$n, names.arg = drinks$beverage,
        col = c("tan4", "darkseagreen", "grey70"), border = NA,
        main = "What the class drinks", ylab = "Students")









genres <- class |> count(genre, sort = TRUE)

par(mar = c(4, 11, 3, 1))                       # room for long labels on the left
barplot(rev(genres$n), names.arg = rev(genres$genre), horiz = TRUE, las = 1,
        col = "steelblue", border = NA,
        main = "Favourite game genre", xlab = "Students")







par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))                        # back to the default margins

Question. Merge Horror with Survival Horror? What is the unlabelled bar? (Your call, but write it down. The bar is the student with no genre.)
Step 8. Filter: ask about some of the class

# Who are the coffee drinkers?
class |>
  filter(beverage == "Coffee") |>
  select(height, type, genre)

   height type                genre
1     182 INTP First-Person Shooter
2     166 ENFP           Platformer
3     174 INFP               Horror
4     186 ESTP First-Person Shooter
5     180 INTP            Adventure
6     172 INFP            Roguelike
7     178 ISTP First-Person Shooter
8     183 ENTP              Sandbox
9     176 INTP                 <NA>
10    179 INFP         Metroidvania

# Everyone 180 cm or taller: what do they play?
class |>
  filter(height >= 180) |>
  count(genre)

                 genre n
1            Adventure 1
2 First-Person Shooter 2
3              Sandbox 1


Step 9. Groups: does height differ by drink?

class |>
  group_by(beverage) |>
  summarise(n             = sum(!is.na(height)),
            median_height = median(height, na.rm = TRUE),
            iqr_height    = IQR(height, na.rm = TRUE))

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  beverage     n median_height iqr_height
  <chr>    <int>         <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Coffee      10          178.        7  
2 Neither      3          175         9  
3 Tea          6          168.        5.5



boxplot(height ~ beverage, data = class,
        col = c("tan", "grey80", "darkseagreen"), outline = FALSE,  # groups sort A-Z: Coffee, Neither, Tea
        main = "Height by preferred drink", xlab = NULL, ylab = "Height (cm)")
stripchart(height ~ beverage, data = class, vertical = TRUE, add = TRUE,
           method = "jitter", jitter = 0.1, pch = 19,
           col = adjustcolor("grey20", alpha.f = 0.6))








Question. Coffee drinkers’ median is about 10 cm taller. Real? (Check n first: 10, 6 and 3. Too few to say. That is the Stage 2 question.)
Step 10. Two categories together

class |>
  count(mind, beverage)

       mind beverage n
1 Extravert   Coffee 3
2 Extravert      Tea 2
3 Introvert   Coffee 7
4 Introvert  Neither 3
5 Introvert      Tea 5

# barplot() wants a table with groups in rows; table() builds one.
drink_by_mind <- table(class$beverage, class$mind)

barplot(drink_by_mind, beside = TRUE,
        col = c("tan", "grey80", "darkseagreen"), border = NA,  # Coffee, Neither, Tea
        legend.text = TRUE, args.legend = list(x = "topleft", bty = "n"),
        main = "Preferred drink, by introvert or extravert", ylab = "Students")








The same table as a mosaic plot: each tile’s area is its share of the class, so the size of each group is part of the picture.

mosaicplot(table(class$mind, class$beverage),
           color = c("tan", "grey80", "darkseagreen"),   # Coffee, Neither, Tea
           main = "Drink by introvert or extravert", xlab = "", ylab = "")








Question. Which chart shows the 15 to 5 split better? (The mosaic. And with 5 extraverts, one person moves their whole picture.)
Step 11. Pictures for a small class
With twenty students, the best pictures show every student, or every answer, rather than a distribution. First, the whole class’s personality profile: the share holding the first letter of each pair.

# One summary per letter pair: the share of the class with the first letter.
balance <- class |>
  summarise(E = mean(substr(type, 1, 1) == "E"),
            N = mean(substr(type, 2, 2) == "N"),
            T = mean(substr(type, 3, 3) == "T"),
            J = mean(substr(type, 4, 4) == "J"))
balance

     E   N   T    J
1 0.25 0.7 0.5 0.35

first  <- unlist(balance)           # the four shares as a plain vector
shares <- rbind(first, 1 - first)   # row 1: first letter, row 2: the other letter

par(mar = c(4, 12, 3, 1))   # room for the long labels on the left
bars <- barplot(shares, horiz = TRUE, las = 1, border = NA,
                col = c("steelblue", "grey85"),
                names.arg = c("Extravert / Introvert", "Intuitive / Sensing",
                              "Thinking / Feeling", "Judging / Perceiving"),
                main = "The class's personality profile", xlab = "Share of the class")
abline(v = 0.5, lty = 2)
text(first / 2, bars, c("E", "N", "T", "J"), col = "white", font = 2)
text(first + (1 - first) / 2, bars, c("I", "S", "F", "P"), font = 2)







par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))

Question. Which pair is most even, which most lopsided? (Thinking / Feeling is even; Extravert / Introvert is one to three. Four pairs work because 16 types are too thin.)
Second, every student’s height, shortest to tallest, coloured by drink:

by_height <- class |>
  filter(!is.na(height)) |>   # a student with no height has no dot to draw
  arrange(height)

# A named vector works as a lookup: drink_col["Tea"] gives "darkseagreen".
drink_col <- c(Coffee = "tan4", Tea = "darkseagreen", Neither = "grey60")

dotchart(by_height$height, labels = paste("Student", by_height$id),
         pch = 19, cex = 0.8, col = drink_col[by_height$beverage],
         main = "Every student, shortest to tallest", xlab = "Height (cm)")
legend("bottomright", legend = names(drink_col), col = drink_col,
       pch = 19, bty = "n")








Question. What does this show that the histogram hid? (Every student, and the tall end is mostly coffee.) Everything you just did is Stage 1. Next: a playtest.
