title: Stage 2 Demo
text:
Demo 1 — Cleaning is analysis
Step 1. Read the export as delivered

library(readr)
library(dplyr)

# trim_ws = FALSE: see the stray spaces Excel would see. read_csv hides them.
raw <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_sessions_raw.csv",
                trim_ws = FALSE, show_col_types = FALSE)
nrow(raw)   # 120 sessions were played

[1] 124


Step 2. Rows exported twice

nrow(raw) - nrow(distinct(raw))              # rows repeating every column

[1] 4

raw |> count(session_id) |> filter(n > 1)    # keys appearing twice: the same ones

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  session_id     n
  <chr>      <int>
1 S046           2
2 S053           2
3 S057           2
4 S103           2

clean <- raw |> distinct()                   # keep the first copy of each
nrow(clean)

[1] 120


Step 3. Labels that should match

clean |> count(cohort)   # spaces and capitals make extra "cohorts"

# A tibble: 13 × 2
   cohort         n
   <chr>      <int>
 1 " Novice"      1
 2 " Regular"     1
 3 " Veteran"     1
 4 "Novice"      30
 5 "Novice "      2
 6 "REGULAR"      3
 7 "Regular"     45
 8 "Regular "     3
 9 "VETERAN"      1
10 "Veteran"     27
11 "Veteran "     2
12 "regular"      1
13 "veteran"      3

clean <- clean |> mutate(cohort = tolower(trimws(cohort)))
clean |> count(cohort)   # always check the fix by counting again

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  cohort      n
  <chr>   <int>
1 novice     33
2 regular    53
3 veteran    34


Step 4. Where the gaps are

colSums(is.na(clean))   # blanks per column

       session_id         player_id            cohort         archetype 
                0                 0                 0                 0 
            build          accuracy          mobility     survivability 
                0                 0                 0                 0 
objective_control           support         awareness             score 
                0                 0                 0                 0 
            kills            deaths        objectives       shots_fired 
                0                 3                 0                 0 
     time_alive_s        distance_m   session_minutes       quit_reason 
                0                 0                 8                 0 
      wrong_turns   items_collected         completed        difficulty 
                0                 0                 0                 0 
        enjoyment           comment 
                0                 0 

# Split the blank session lengths by something that might explain them.
clean |>
  filter(is.na(session_minutes)) |>
  count(build, quit_reason)

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  build quit_reason     n
  <chr> <chr>       <int>
1 A     Frustrated      8


Question. Every blank session length is a Build A frustration quit. Noise, or a finding?
Step 5. The one-line fix that removes the finding

kept <- clean[complete.cases(clean), ]   # "just drop the NAs", as people often do
nrow(kept)

[1] 109

clean |> filter(quit_reason == "Frustrated") |> count(build)   # before

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  build     n
  <chr> <int>
1 A        20
2 B         5

kept  |> filter(quit_reason == "Frustrated") |> count(build)   # after

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  build     n
  <chr> <int>
1 A        12
2 B         5


Question. Nothing warned us. What goes in the cleaning log?
Step 6. The six verbs, read as a sentence

# The pipe passes the left-hand result in as the first argument on the right.
clean |>
  filter(build == "A", quit_reason == "Frustrated") |>
  mutate(logged = !is.na(session_minutes)) |>
  select(session_id, cohort, session_minutes, logged) |>
  arrange(session_minutes) |>
  head(4)

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  session_id cohort  session_minutes logged
  <chr>      <chr>             <dbl> <lgl> 
1 S117       regular             8.6 TRUE  
2 S043       novice              9.3 TRUE  
3 S097       novice              9.6 TRUE  
4 S039       regular            10.3 TRUE  


Step 7. Split, apply, combine

# Split by build, apply each summary, combine into one row per build.
clean |>
  group_by(build) |>
  summarise(n          = n(),
            mean_wrong = mean(wrong_turns),
            missing    = sum(is.na(session_minutes)))

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  build     n mean_wrong missing
  <chr> <int>      <dbl>   <int>
1 A        60       8.92       8

Question. Which of these numbers goes in the cleaning log?

title: Stage 2 Demo
section: Demo 2 — Is the difference real, and does it matter?
text:
Demo 2 — Is the difference real, and does it matter?
Step 8. Look before you test

# The complete export: same sessions, logging fault fixed.
sessions <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_sessions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

boxplot(wrong_turns ~ build, data = sessions,
        main = "Wrong turns by build", ylab = "Wrong turns", col = "grey85")








Step 9. Another playtest, another answer

# Pretend we could only afford 15 sessions per build. Draw five such playtests.
set.seed(8015)
replicate(5, {
  a <- sample(sessions$wrong_turns[sessions$build == "A"], 15)
  b <- sample(sessions$wrong_turns[sessions$build == "B"], 15)
  mean(a) - mean(b)  # the difference this playtest would have reported
})

[1] 4.066667 3.733333 3.866667 3.466667 5.200000



# Now a thousand of them: the sampling distribution of the difference.
set.seed(8015)
diffs <- replicate(1000, {
  a <- sample(sessions$wrong_turns[sessions$build == "A"], 15)
  b <- sample(sessions$wrong_turns[sessions$build == "B"], 15)
  mean(a) - mean(b)
})
hist(diffs, breaks = 30, col = "grey85", border = "white",
     main = "1,000 playtests of 15 per build", xlab = "Difference in mean wrong turns")







sd(diffs)  # the standard error, seen directly

[1] 0.7831418


Question. Same builds, a thousand answers. Which one is “the” difference? Its spread is the standard error, which the t-test estimates from one sample. The students do not write this code; the picture is the point.
Step 10. Shuffle the labels: what does chance alone produce?

# If the build made no difference, its label would be arbitrary. Shuffle it.
gap <- function(y, g) mean(y[g == "A"]) - mean(y[g == "B"])
observed <- gap(sessions$wrong_turns, sessions$build)

set.seed(1)
shuffled <- replicate(10000, gap(sessions$wrong_turns, sample(sessions$build)))

hist(shuffled, breaks = 40, col = "grey85", border = "white",
     xlim = range(c(shuffled, observed)),
     main = "Gaps from shuffled build labels", xlab = "Difference (A - B)")
abline(v = observed, col = "firebrick", lwd = 3)







mean(abs(shuffled) >= abs(observed))  # the p-value: share of shuffles this extreme

[1] 0


Question. Not one shuffle in ten thousand got near the real gap. What does that say about “it was just the players we happened to get”? That share is what every p-value means.
Step 11. The t-test: size, interval, p-value

# Different players on each build, so the independent-samples test.
result <- t.test(wrong_turns ~ build, data = sessions)
result


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  wrong_turns by build
t = 7.3208, df = 116.07, p-value = 3.492e-11
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group A and group B is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 2.480141 4.319859
sample estimates:
mean in group A mean in group B 
       8.916667        5.516667 

result$estimate  # 1-2. what happened, and how large?

mean in group A mean in group B 
       8.916667        5.516667 

result$conf.int  # 3. how uncertain? read this before the p-value

[1] 2.480141 4.319859
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

result$p.value   # 4. could a gap this big be chance alone?

[1] 3.491687e-11


Question. Does a difference this size matter to a player, and what should the team do?
Step 12. Same players, both builds

paired <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_paired.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Paired: each player compared with themselves, so player skill cancels out.
t.test(paired$wrong_turns_a, paired$wrong_turns_b, paired = TRUE)$conf.int

[1] 1.838014 3.695319
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

# Same data, wrongly treated as two separate groups: a much wider interval.
t.test(paired$wrong_turns_a, paired$wrong_turns_b)$conf.int

[1] 1.180570 4.352763
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95


Step 13. Significant is not the same as important

# Build B was rated harder, and the result is significant...
harder <- t.test(difficulty ~ build, data = sessions)
harder


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  difficulty by build
t = -2.175, df = 117.47, p-value = 0.03163
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group A and group B is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.7960481 -0.0372852
sample estimates:
mean in group A mean in group B 
       3.916667        4.333333 

# ...but the players did not actually die more.
t.test(deaths ~ build, data = sessions)$p.value

[1] 0.6793394


Question. Build B was rated under half a point harder on a seven-point scale, and deaths did not change. Would you act on it? What would you check in the next playtest?

Question. Build B took far fewer wrong turns, yet more of its players wrote that they were lost. Which evidence do we trust for what? Where does this go in the report: Results, Discussion, or both?
Step 5. The report skeleton
The report is a .qmd file: the eight assessment headings, a hidden setup chunk, and numbers written as inline R.

title: "Tidebreak Build B: Playtest Report"
---

```{r}
#| echo: false
sessions <- readr::read_csv("data/tidebreak_sessions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

## Executive Summary
## Introduction
## Methodology

We analysed `r nrow(sessions)` sessions.

## Results
## Discussion

## References
## Appendices
Step 6. Watch the inline numbers recompute

# One sentence of the Methodology, with its numbers as inline R.
part2 <- paste(
  "We analysed `r nrow(sessions)` sessions. Build A's median session lasted",
  "`r median(sessions$session_minutes[sessions$build == 'A'], na.rm = TRUE)` minutes."
)

# render_text() does to this sentence what quarto render does to the report.
render_text(part2)   # against the full data...


We analysed 120 sessions. Build A's median session lasted 23.25 minutes.

# ...then against Stage 2's raw export with incomplete rows dropped.
raw <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_sessions_raw.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
sessions <- raw[!duplicated(raw), ]
sessions <- sessions[complete.cases(sessions), ]

render_text(part2)


We analysed 109 sessions. Build A's median session lasted 25.5 minutes.


Question. Which of those two sentences would have gone into the report if the numbers were typed by hand? Then: open your own report.qmd.

title: Regression
text: Going further. This page extends Relationships and Correlation. Nothing here is needed for the labs or the assessment. Read it if your team wants to say how much one measure changes with another, or if a residual might be hiding your finding.

title: Regression
text:
Simple Linear Regression
Correlation says how tightly two variables follow a line. Simple linear regression finds that line, and so answers a more useful question: how much does one variable change, on average, for each unit of the other?

fit <- lm(score ~ awareness, data = sessions)
coef(fit)

(Intercept)   awareness 
  426.13072    15.15319 

confint(fit)

               2.5 %    97.5 %
(Intercept) 172.1697 680.09176
awareness    11.3806  18.92578


lm() stands for linear model. score ~ awareness reads “score as explained by awareness”, the same formula style as boxplot(y ~ group). The result describes a straight line:
\[\text{predicted score} = 426 + 15.2 \times \text{awareness}\]
The slope is the number that matters: each extra point of awareness goes with 15.2 more points of score, on average (95% CI 11.4 to 18.9). It is in the units of the question, so a designer can use it: the 18-point gap in average awareness between Novices and Veterans goes with about 280 points of score.
The intercept is the predicted score at awareness zero: 426. No player has an awareness anywhere near zero (the lowest is 38), so it means nothing on its own; it just anchors the line.

title: Regression
text:
Residuals

sessions$predicted <- fitted(fit)
sessions$residual  <- resid(fit)
ggplot(sessions, aes(awareness, score)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = awareness, yend = predicted), colour = "grey75") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = residual < -600), size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = pal$highlight) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = pal$line, `TRUE` = "#8a5a9c"),
                      labels = c("Other sessions", "Residual below −600"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Awareness rating", y = "Score") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")







Figure 1: Score against awareness, with the regression line. Each grey segment is a residual; the sessions furthest below the line are mostly Sentinel collapses.





A residual is the gap between what actually happened and what the line predicted: actual minus predicted. The line is chosen to make the residuals, taken together, as small as possible (it minimises the sum of their squares, hence “least squares”). geom_smooth(method = "lm") draws the same line.
Residuals are where the findings hide. The seven sessions furthest below the line, the ones that scored far less than their awareness predicted, include 6 Sentinels. The regression has found the Sentinel collapses from Describing Variables on its own: those games are not explained by awareness at all.

sessions[order(resid(fit))[1:7], c("session_id", "archetype", "awareness", "score")]

# A tibble: 7 × 4
  session_id archetype awareness score
  <chr>      <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 S059       Sentinel         78   587
2 S045       Sentinel         63   597
3 S034       Sentinel         61   584

title: Regression
text:
R²
R², the coefficient of determination, is the share of the variation in score that the line accounts for: 0.35, or 35%. For a simple regression it is exactly the correlation squared (0.59² = 0.35). Awareness accounts for about a third of the differences in score; the other two thirds are everything else.

title: Regression
text:
Predicting, Carefully
The line predicts a score of about 1640 for awareness 80. That prediction is an average for players like that, not a promise for any one player, whose residual could easily be 260 points either way. And never predict outside the data: the line knows nothing about awareness below 38 or above 95. Using it there is extrapolation, and the straight line may not continue.
A regression is still a correlation. A steep, significant slope says awareness and score move together, by this much. It does not say that raising a player’s awareness would raise their score. Every warning about confounding applies unchanged.

title: Regression
text:
Reading the Full Summary
summary(fit) prints everything at once:

summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = score ~ awareness, data = sessions)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-1021.08   -97.01    18.49   183.27   436.30 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  426.131    128.246   3.323  0.00119 ** 
awareness     15.153      1.905   7.954 1.22e-12 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 258.6 on 118 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.349, Adjusted R-squared:  0.3435 
F-statistic: 63.27 on 1 and 118 DF,  p-value: 1.223e-12


The awareness row of the Coefficients table gives the slope, its standard error and a p-value testing whether the true slope could be zero. Multiple R-squared is R². Regression with several predictors at once (multiple regression) can adjust for a confounder such as cohort, but it is beyond this course, and adjusting for the confounders you measured does not protect you from the ones you did not.

title: Regression
text:
Try It

Fit a regression of score on deaths. Interpret the slope in one sentence a designer could use, and compare its R² with awareness’s.
A designer reads the awareness regression and says: “If we raise a Novice’s awareness by 20 points, they will score about 300 more.” Give two reasons to doubt it.







NoteShow answers





1.

fit_d <- lm(score ~ deaths, data = sessions)
coef(fit_d)

(Intercept)      deaths 
  1779.8824   -116.7144 

summary(fit_d)$r.squared

[1] 0.3156496


Each extra death goes with about 117 fewer points of score, on average. R² is 0.32, a little below awareness’s 0.35. The same caution applies: dying more and scoring less may both come from being outplayed.
2. First, the slope is an association across players, not the effect of changing one player: awareness ratings may reflect skill rather than cause it. Second, it is an average: individual players scatter around the line by about 260 points. A third reason, if the Novice starts low: their raised awareness may still be in a range where the data is thin.

title: Sampling Theory
text: Going further. This page extends From Sample to Population. Nothing here is needed for the labs or the assessment. Read it if you want to know why the standard error and the confidence interval work, or if you need an interval for something other than a mean.

title: Sampling Theory
text:
The Standard Error Formula
The standard error can be estimated from a single sample:
\[\text{SE} = \frac{\text{SD}}{\sqrt{n}}\]
Check it against the simulation on the notes page. The population SD is 7.73, so for n = 30 the formula gives 7.73 / √30 = 1.41. The SD of a thousand simulated playtest means is 1.37. The formula works.
Bigger samples give smaller standard errors, but slowly. Because n is under a square root, you need four times the players to halve the standard error:

par(mar = c(4, 6, 1, 1))
stripchart(list("n = 10" = means_10, "n = 30" = means_30, "n = 100" = means_100),
           method = "jitter", jitter = 0.25, pch = 16, cex = 0.4, las = 1,
           col = adjustcolor(pal$line, alpha.f = 0.3),
           xlab = "Playtest mean session length (minutes)")
abline(v = pop_mean, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = pal$highlight)







Figure 1: Means of 1,000 simulated playtests at three sizes. Each quadrupling of n roughly halves the spread.













Players per playtest

title: Sampling Theory
text:
The Central Limit Theorem
Session length is lopsided and two-humped, nothing like a bell. Yet the means of playtests drawn from it form a bell almost perfectly:

par(mar = c(4, 3, 1, 1))
hist(means_30, breaks = 30, freq = FALSE, col = pal$fill, border = "white",
     main = "", xlab = "Mean session length (minutes)", ylab = "", yaxt = "n")
curve(dnorm(x, mean(means_30), sd(means_30)), add = TRUE, lwd = 2,
      col = pal$highlight)







Figure 2: The means of 1,000 playtests of 30, with a normal curve laid over them. The individual sessions are far from normal; their means are not.





That is the central limit theorem: whatever shape the individual values have, the means of reasonably large samples are approximately normal.
It is why the normal distribution matters even for data that is not normal. The 68–95–99.7 rule does not describe the session lengths, but it does describe the sampling distribution of their mean. So about 95% of playtest means fall within 2 standard errors of the true mean. That single fact is what confidence intervals and t-tests are built on.
How large is “reasonably large”? For mildly skewed data, 30 is usually plenty. For heavily skewed data, such as frame times with rare hitches, it takes more. And it applies to means: it does not rescue a 99th percentile.

title: Sampling Theory
text:
The Interval by Hand
The “about 2” in “mean ± about 2 SE” is 1.96 for large samples. For smaller ones R uses a slightly larger number from the t distribution, which allows for the SD itself being estimated from the sample. The part after the ± is the margin of error.

m  <- mean(mins_b)
se <- sd(mins_b) / sqrt(length(mins_b))
multiplier <- qt(0.975, df = length(mins_b) - 1)

c(mean = m, se = se, multiplier = multiplier)

      mean         se multiplier 
24.2416667  0.8962864  2.0009954 

m + c(-1, 1) * multiplier * se

[1] 22.44820 26.03513


The same as t.test(mins_b)$conf.int: 22.4 to 26.
\[\text{95\% CI} = \bar{x} \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1} \times \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]
A 99% interval uses a larger multiplier, so it is wider: more confidence costs precision.

title: Sampling Theory
text:
The Bootstrap
The formula relies on the central limit theorem. The bootstrap gets an interval without it, by treating your sample as a stand-in for the population and resampling it. Draw 60 sessions with replacement from Build B’s 60, take the mean, and repeat a thousand times; the middle 95% of those means is the interval.

set.seed(3)
boot_means <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(mins_b, replace = TRUE)))
quantile(boot_means, c(0.025, 0.975))

    2.5%    97.5% 
22.59825 25.83671 


It agrees closely with t.test()’s 22.4 to 26. The bootstrap earns its keep for summaries with no simple formula, such as a median or a 99th percentile: replace mean with median in the line above and it still works.

set.seed(3)
boot_medians <- replicate(1000, median(sample(mins_b, replace = TRUE)))
quantile(boot_medians, c(0.025, 0.975))

   2.5%   97.5% 
24.7975 28.1500

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
text:
These are the questions that come up in the week after a playtest. None of them is exotic. All of them are painful to answer with a spreadsheet, and each one is answered below by a single figure and a few dozen lines of R.



The question you are actually asking
Answered by




I have 120 rows of results and no idea what is in them. Where do I start?
View 1


All four characters average about the same score. Does that mean they are balanced?
View 2


I designed four classes to play differently. Did they stay different once real people played them?
View 3


I want players to score higher. Which ability is actually worth buffing?
View 4


Testers keep giving up partway through. When do I lose them, and is it the same moment every time?
View 5


The survey came back with 960 ratings across eight questions. Which complaint do I fix first?
View 6


My frame-rate counter says 60 FPS. My testers say the game stutters. Who is lying?
View 7


How can I find where players are loitering, sniping, or being funnelled into a kill zone?
View 8


Which parts of my level is nobody using?
View 8


How did one particular player move through the level — did they learn the route, or wander?
View 8b



Every one of these is a question about your own game, asked of data your own engine can already record. The only thing missing is the ability to read it.

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
text:
Before you read any code
This document is a showcase, not a lesson. Nothing here is examinable and you are not expected to understand the code yet. Its only job is to show you what a few months of R can do to a pile of raw playtest numbers.
Every figure below was produced from 5 CSV files, in chunks of between 11 and 55 lines of code. By the end of these notes you will be able to answer the first seven questions with base R, dplyr and ggplot2, producing plainer, static versions of the plots shown here. The three movement questions in View 8 use position data that stays in this showcase. The polish on this page is the destination, not the syllabus.
To begin the notes, go to Start Here. It explains the four stages of the course, from October to March, and how the notes, labs and reference pages fit together.






NoteThe data



Tidebreak is a fictional four-player top-down arena, used here so that the example is self-contained. The playtest recorded four things:








File
One row per
Holds




tidebreak_sessions.csv
player, per session
Six end-of-match ability ratings, match statistics, wrong turns, items collected, whether the session was completed, session length, quit reason, difficulty and enjoyment ratings, and a one-line comment, for 120 sessions


tidebreak_survey.csv
player, per session
Eight agreement items rated 1 to 5


tidebreak_frame_times.csv
rendered frame
Frame time in milliseconds, by build and level zone


tidebreak_positions.csv
player, per second
Top-down position for eight players across one 180-second match



All four are synthetic, but they behave like the real thing: the numbers are messy, the interesting findings are not the obvious ones, and at least two widely held assumptions about the game turn out to be wrong.




Show the code
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
library(DT)

# Five files from one playtest. Everything below comes from these.
sessions    <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_sessions.csv")
survey      <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_survey.csv")
frame_times <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_frame_times.csv")
positions   <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_positions.csv")
level       <- read_csv("data/tidebreak_level.csv")

# A handful of colours, used everywhere. Fewer colours, fewer things to learn.
pal <- c(blue = "#2a78d6", orange = "#eb6834", aqua = "#1baf7a", yellow = "#eda100")
ink <- c(primary = "#0b0b0b", secondary = "#52514e", grid = "#e6e5e1")

# Each archetype keeps its colour in every view, so blue always means Scout.
arch_pal <- c(Scout = pal[["blue"]],  Sentinel = pal[["orange"]],
              Engineer = pal[["aqua"]], Duelist = pal[["yellow"]])

# Same idea for the two builds, which come back in Views 5 and 7.
build_pal <- c(A = pal[["orange"]], B = pal[["blue"]])

# One shared look for every chart, so the views read as one document.
theme_tb <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ink["primary"], size = 13),
      plot.subtitle   = element_text(colour = ink["secondary"], size = 11),
      axis.title      = element_text(colour = ink["secondary"], size = 10),
      axis.text       = element_text(colour = ink["secondary"]),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = ink["grid"], linewidth = 0.3),
      legend.position = "none"
    )
}

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
section: View 1 — The table you can actually read
text:
View 1 — The table you can actually read
Question: what happened in each session?
Before you analyse anything you need to be able to look at your data. A raw CSV in Excel is awkward at 120 rows and unusable at 120,000. A rendered table is searchable and sortable, and it goes straight into a report.
Sort by Score, or type Sentinel into the search box, and you will already see the finding that View 2 makes formal.


Show the code
sessions %>%
  # Keep the ten columns a designer asks about first, with readable names.
  select(Session = session_id, Player = player_id, Cohort = cohort,
         Archetype = archetype, Build = build, Score = score,
         Kills = kills, Deaths = deaths, `Alive (s)` = time_alive_s,
         Awareness = awareness) %>%
  # datatable() turns it into a table you can search, sort and page through.
  datatable(
    rownames = FALSE,
    options  = list(pageLength = 8, dom = "ftip", scrollX = TRUE),
    caption  = "Tidebreak playtest: 120 sessions"
  ) %>%
  # A bar inside each Score cell, so high and low scores jump out as you scroll.
  formatStyle("Score",
    background = styleColorBar(range(sessions$score), "#cde2fb"),
    backgroundSize = "98% 60%", backgroundRepeat = "no-repeat",
    backgroundPosition = "center")

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
text:
View 2 — Distributions, not averages
Question: which archetype performs best?
The tempting answer is to compare four average scores. Do that here and the archetypes look almost identical, which would be a design decision made on a misreading.
A violin plot draws the whole distribution. Read the Sentinel shape: it is not one hump but two. Sentinel runs either anchor the objective and score well, or collapse in the opening seconds and score badly. There is almost no middle. That is a balance problem an average would have hidden completely.


Show the code
sessions %>%
  # Order the archetypes by median score, weakest to strongest.
  mutate(archetype = fct_reorder(archetype, score, .fun = median)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(archetype, score, fill = archetype)) +
  # The violin is the whole distribution. Look at the Sentinel: two humps,
  # where an average would show you one.
  geom_violin(colour = NA, alpha = 0.85, width = 0.9) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, fill = "white", colour = ink[["secondary"]],
               outlier.shape = NA, linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = arch_pal) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  # Put the finding in the title, so nobody has to work it out.
  labs(
    title    = "Sentinel is bimodal: it either anchors the round or dies in it",
    subtitle = "Score distribution by archetype, 30 sessions each. Box shows median and interquartile range.",
    x = NULL, y = "Score"
  ) +
  theme_tb()

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
section: View 3 — Six numbers as a shape
text:
View 3 — Six numbers as a shape
Question: are the four archetypes actually playing differently?
Each session ends with six ability ratings on a 0–100 scale. Comparing four archetypes across six measures means twenty-four numbers, which no one can hold in their head. Drawn as a radar, each archetype becomes a shape you can recognise at a glance, and the grey outline behind each one is the all-player average for reference.
The shapes are distinct and they are roughly the shapes the design intended. That is the result you want from this chart: confirmation that the archetypes are not quietly converging on the same playstyle.


Show the code
metrics <- c("accuracy", "mobility", "survivability",
             "objective_control", "support", "awareness")

pretty <- c(accuracy = "Accuracy", mobility = "Mobility",
            survivability = "Survival", objective_control = "Objective",
            support = "Support", awareness = "Awareness")

# One row per archetype per ability, so every ability can sit on the same circle.
long <- sessions %>%
  select(archetype, all_of(metrics)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-archetype, names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(metric = factor(pretty[metric], levels = unname(pretty)))

# The average for each archetype, and for everyone, to draw against.
by_arch <- long %>% group_by(archetype, metric) %>% summarise(value = mean(value))
overall <- long %>% group_by(metric) %>% summarise(value = mean(value))

ggplot() +
  # Grey outline: the all-player average. Coloured shape: one archetype.
  geom_polygon(data = overall, aes(metric, value, group = 1),
               fill = NA, colour = ink[["grid"]], linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_polygon(data = by_arch,
               aes(metric, value, group = archetype, fill = archetype, colour = archetype),
               alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = by_arch, aes(metric, value, colour = archetype), size = 1.8) +
  # coord_polar() bends the axis into a circle. That is all a radar chart is.
  coord_polar(clip = "off") +
  facet_wrap(~archetype, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = arch_pal) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = arch_pal) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), breaks = c(25, 50, 75)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Four archetypes, four distinct ability profiles",
    subtitle = "Mean end-of-match rating per ability. Grey outline is the all-player average.",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_tb() +
  theme(axis.text.y   = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x   = element_text(size = 7),
        strip.text    = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ink[["primary"]]),
        panel.spacing = unit(1.6, "lines"),
        plot.margin   = margin(10, 20, 10, 20))

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
text:
View 4 — What actually drives score
Question: which abilities and behaviours move the scoreboard?
A correlogram puts every pair of variables in one picture. Blue means the two rise together, red means one rises as the other falls, and pale means no relationship at all.
Three things to read off it:

Awareness is the strongest positive correlate of score. Map knowledge beats mechanical skill in this build.
Shots fired is essentially uncorrelated with score. Players who shoot more do not win more, which contradicts what the team assumed.
Mobility and survivability pull against each other, which is the intended trade-off working as designed.



Show the code
vars <- c("accuracy", "mobility", "survivability", "objective_control",
          "support", "awareness", "shots_fired", "distance_m",
          "kills", "deaths", "objectives", "score")

nice <- c(accuracy = "Accuracy", mobility = "Mobility", survivability = "Survival",
          objective_control = "Objective ctrl", support = "Support",
          awareness = "Awareness", shots_fired = "Shots fired",
          distance_m = "Distance", kills = "Kills", deaths = "Deaths",
          objectives = "Objectives", score = "Score")

# Every measure correlated with every other one.
cm <- cor(sessions[vars])
# Sit measures that move together next to each other, so the clusters stand out.
ord <- hclust(as.dist(1 - cm))$order
lv  <- nice[vars[ord]]

cm_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(cm)) %>%
  setNames(c("a", "b", "r")) %>%
  mutate(a = factor(nice[as.character(a)], levels = lv),
         b = factor(nice[as.character(b)], levels = lv)) %>%
  filter(as.integer(a) < as.integer(b))   # keep one half: the other is a mirror image

ggplot(cm_long, aes(a, b, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +
  # Print each value. White text on the dark squares, so it stays readable.
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", r),
                colour = abs(r) > 0.55), size = 2.9) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#e34948", mid = "#f0efec", high = "#2a78d6",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1), name = "r") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = ink[["secondary"]]),
                      guide = "none") +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(
    title    = "Awareness drives score; shots fired does not",
    subtitle = "Pearson correlation between every pair of measures, 120 sessions.",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_tb() +
  theme(axis.text.x       = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        legend.position   = "right",
        panel.grid.major  = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor  = element_blank())

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
text:
View 5 — When people stop playing
Question: we changed how the game explains its objective. Did it keep anyone?
A retention curve shows what fraction of participants were still playing at each minute of the test. It is the shape that matters, not the endpoint: a smooth decay means people drifted away, a cliff means something specific pushed them out.
Build A has a cliff. Between minutes 11 and 13 it drops from 88% to 68%, and 15 of the 17 people who left in that window are logged as frustration quits. Build B, which explains its objective differently, is still at 90% at minute 13 and loses five people to frustration across the whole test against Build A’s twenty.
Now look at what a summary table would have told you: median session length is 23.2 minutes for Build A and 27.1 for Build B. That reads as a modest improvement. The curve shows something else — one specific, fixable moment where a fifth of the Build A testers gave up.


Show the code
# Check every quarter-minute of the 32-minute session.
minutes <- seq(0, 32, by = 0.25)

# For each build and each moment: what share of sessions were still going?
retention <- map_dfr(c("A", "B"), function(b) {
  lengths <- sessions %>% filter(build == b) %>% pull(session_minutes)
  tibble(build = b, minute = minutes,
         pct = map_dbl(minutes, ~ 100 * mean(lengths >= .x)))
})

ends <- retention %>% group_by(build) %>% slice_max(minute, n = 1)

ggplot(retention, aes(minute, pct, colour = build)) +
  # Shade minutes 11 to 13. That's where Build A loses its players.
  annotate("rect", xmin = 11, xmax = 13, ymin = 0, ymax = 100,
           fill = ink[["grid"]], alpha = 0.55) +
  annotate("text", x = 13.4, y = 24, hjust = 0, size = 3.2,
           colour = ink[["secondary"]],
           label = "88% to 68% in two minutes,\nalmost all frustration quits") +
  # Steps, not a smooth line: players leave at a moment, not gradually.
  geom_step(linewidth = 1.1, direction = "hv") +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = paste0("Build ", build)),
            hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.6, size = 3.6, fontface = "bold",
            show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = build_pal) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 37), breaks = seq(0, 30, 5),
                     labels = function(x) paste0(x, " min")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), labels = function(y) paste0(y, "%")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Build A loses people at a cliff; Build B does not",
    subtitle = "Percentage of participants still playing, by minute of the test session.",
    x = NULL, y = "Still playing"
  ) +
  theme_tb()

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
section: View 6 — What players said, ranked by how badly it went
text:
View 6 — What players said, ranked by how badly it went
Question: the survey has eight questions and 120 responses. Which one should we act on first?
Eight averages tell you almost nothing, because a mean of 3.0 can mean everyone was indifferent or that half loved it and half hated it. A diverging bar chart splits each item at the neutral response: disagreement runs left, agreement runs right, and the items sort by the net.
The result is uncomfortable in the way real survey results usually are. The art is the best-rated thing in the game by a distance. The worst-rated item is whether players ever knew what they were supposed to be doing — the same thing that drives the cliff in View 5. People praise the visuals and quit over the design.


Show the code
item_label <- c(
  objective_clear     = "I always knew what my objective was",
  death_understood    = "I understood why I died",
  difficulty_fair     = "The difficulty felt fair",
  level_navigable     = "The level was easy to navigate",
  would_play_again    = "I would play this again",
  match_length        = "The match length felt right",
  controls_responsive = "The controls felt responsive",
  visual_style        = "The visual style is appealing"
)

resp_label <- c("Strongly disagree", "Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree", "Strongly agree")

# One row per answer, then the share of each rating for every question.
props <- survey %>%
  pivot_longer(-session_id, names_to = "item", values_to = "resp") %>%
  count(item, resp) %>%
  complete(item, resp = 1:5, fill = list(n = 0)) %>%
  group_by(item) %>% mutate(pct = 100 * n / sum(n)) %>% ungroup()

# Sort the questions by net agreement, agree minus disagree. Worst at the bottom.
ranking <- props %>%
  group_by(item) %>%
  summarise(net = sum(pct[resp >= 4]) - sum(pct[resp <= 2])) %>%
  arrange(net)

item_levels <- unname(item_label[ranking$item])

# Split the neutral answers in half, so each bar balances on zero.
as_bars <- function(d, sign) {
  d %>%
    mutate(signed = sign * if_else(resp == 3, pct / 2, pct),
           item   = factor(unname(item_label[item]), levels = item_levels),
           resp   = factor(resp_label[resp], levels = resp_label))
}

# Disagreement goes left, agreement goes right, strongest answers on the outside.
bars_neg <- props %>% filter(resp <= 3) %>% as_bars(-1)
bars_pos <- props %>% filter(resp >= 3) %>% as_bars(+1)

ranking <- ranking %>%
  mutate(item = factor(unname(item_label[item]), levels = item_levels))

ggplot(mapping = aes(signed, item, fill = resp)) +
  geom_col(data = bars_neg, width = 0.72, position = position_stack()) +
  geom_col(data = bars_pos, width = 0.72, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#fcfcfb", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_text(data = ranking, aes(x = 106, y = item, label = sprintf("%+.0f", net)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3.3, fontface = "bold",
            colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Strongly disagree" = "#e34948",
                               "Disagree"          = "#f2a9a8",
                               "Neutral"           = "#d9d8d4",
                               "Agree"             = "#9ec5f4",
                               "Strongly agree"    = "#2a78d6")) +
  # Zoom with coord_cartesian(), not scale limits. Limits quietly drop any
  # bar that pokes past the edge.
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-60, 90, 30),
                     labels = function(x) paste0(abs(x), "%")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-68, 112)) +
  labs(
    title    = "They love the art and cannot tell what the game wants",
    subtitle = "Share of 120 responses. Bars pivot on neutral; the number is net agreement.",
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_tb() +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        legend.text     = element_text(size = 9),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
section: View 7 — The frame-rate counter is lying to you
text:
View 7 — The frame-rate counter is lying to you
Question: both builds average about 59 FPS. Testers say Build B stutters. Who is right?
Both are. Average frame rate is a mean, and a mean is exactly the wrong summary for a quantity where the rare bad values are the entire user experience. Build B renders almost every frame slightly faster than Build A. It also renders one frame in every twenty-five — about twice a second — in 35 to 55 ms instead of 17, and only in one zone of the level: the corridor that View 8 identifies as the choke point.
The trace shows it. The table shows why the FPS readout missed it: the two builds are separated by 0.05 ms at the mean and by 20 ms at the 99th percentile.


Show the code
# The first 400 frames of the Corridor, one panel per build.
ggplot(frame_times %>% filter(zone == "Corridor", frame <= 400),
       aes(frame, ms, colour = build)) +
  # Dashed line: the 60 FPS budget, 16.7 ms a frame.
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1000 / 60, linetype = "22",
             colour = ink[["secondary"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.45) +
  facet_wrap(~build, ncol = 1, labeller = labeller(build = function(b) paste("Build", b))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = build_pal) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 60), breaks = c(1000/60, 30, 45, 60),
                     labels = c("16.7\n(60 FPS)", "30", "45", "60")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Identical average, one of them unplayable",
    subtitle = "Frame time in the Corridor zone, first 400 frames. Dashed line is the 60 FPS budget.",
    x = "Frame", y = "Frame time (ms)"
  ) +
  theme_tb() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ink[["primary"]]))











Show the code
# The usual summaries side by side. Watch which columns finally tell the builds apart.
frame_times %>%
  group_by(Build = build) %>%
  summarise(
    `Mean FPS`     = round(1000 / mean(ms), 1),
    `Mean (ms)`    = round(mean(ms), 2),
    `Median (ms)`  = round(median(ms), 1),
    `95th (ms)`    = round(quantile(ms, 0.95), 1),
    `99th (ms)`    = round(quantile(ms, 0.99), 1),
    `Worst (ms)`   = round(max(ms), 1)
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Every column agrees the builds are the same until the last two.")

title: Eight Views of a Playtest
text:
View 8 — Where players actually stand
Question: where are the choke points, the camping spots and the dead space?
This is the figure that changes level layouts. The blue field is total time spent per square metre across the whole match. The moving dots are the eight players, one frame per second, coloured by whether they are moving, loitering or holding position. Dark blocks are cover; the block in the north-east is the raised gantry.
Press play, or drag the slider.
Three readings, all of them actionable:

The gap between the central core and the east block carries almost all lateral traffic, and 14 of the 20 deaths in this match happened inside it. That is a choke point.
Two players spend the entire match holding the north-east gantry. Long dwell, no movement, high kill share: a sniper perch.
The west corner is never visited by anyone. That is floor space the level is paying for and not using.



Show the code
# How long players spent in each 2 m square of the map: the heat underneath.
gx_seq <- seq(1, 59, 2)
gy_seq <- seq(1, 39, 2)

field <- positions %>%
  mutate(gx = floor(x / 2) * 2 + 1, gy = floor(y / 2) * 2 + 1) %>%
  count(gx, gy) %>%
  complete(gx = gx_seq, gy = gy_seq, fill = list(n = 0)) %>%
  arrange(gy, gx)

z <- matrix(field$n, nrow = length(gy_seq), ncol = length(gx_seq), byrow = TRUE)

# The level's walls and raised areas, drawn as rectangles on top.
shapes <- pmap(level, function(block, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, kind) {
  list(type = "rect", x0 = xmin, x1 = xmax, y0 = ymin, y1 = ymax,
       fillcolor = if (kind == "elevated") "#6f6e6a" else "#2f2e2c",
       # The gantry is walkable, so keep it see-through: you can still
       # read the heat underneath.
       opacity = if (kind == "elevated") 0.35 else 0.92,
       line = list(width = 0), layer = "above")
})

# Start the animation at the first second where all three player states
# appear, so the legend is complete from the start.
first_full <- positions %>%
  group_by(t) %>% summarise(k = n_distinct(state)) %>%
  filter(k == 3) %>% slice_min(t) %>% pull(t)

# Every death, to mark with a red cross.
deaths <- positions %>% filter(event == "death")

# plotly makes it interactive: hover for detail, press play to watch the match.
plot_ly(height = 560) %>%
  add_heatmap(
    x = gx_seq, y = gy_seq, z = z, zmin = 0, zmax = 60,
    colorscale = list(c(0, "#fcfcfb"), c(0.25, "#cde2fb"),
                      c(0.6, "#5598e7"), c(1, "#104281")),
    showscale = TRUE, hoverinfo = "z",
    colorbar = list(title = "Seconds\nspent", len = 0.55, thickness = 12,
                    y = 0.72, ticksuffix = "  ")
  ) %>%
  add_markers(
    data = deaths, x = ~x, y = ~y, name = "Death",
    marker = list(symbol = "x", size = 11, color = "#e34948",
                  line = list(color = "#fcfcfb", width = 1)),
    text = ~paste0("death · ", player_id, " · t=", t, "s"), hoverinfo = "text"
  ) %>%
  add_markers(
    data = positions %>% filter(t >= first_full),
    x = ~x, y = ~y, frame = ~t, color = ~state,
    colors = c(Holding = pal[["orange"]], Loitering = pal[["aqua"]],
               Moving = pal[["blue"]]),
    marker = list(size = 13, line = list(color = "#fcfcfb", width = 2)),
    text = ~paste0(player_id, " · t=", t, "s · ", state),
    hoverinfo = "text"
  ) %>%
  layout(
    title  = list(text = "<b>One corridor carries the traffic and most of the deaths</b>",
                  x = 0, font = list(size = 14)),
    shapes = shapes,
    xaxis  = list(title = "x (m)", range = c(0, 60), constrain = "domain"),
    yaxis  = list(title = "y (m)", range = c(0, 40), scaleanchor = "x"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, title = list(text = "")),
    margin = list(t = 80)
  ) %>%
  animation_opts(frame = 90, transition = 45, redraw = FALSE) %>%
  animation_slider(currentvalue = list(prefix = "t = ", suffix = " s"))







Following one player
The map above answers questions about the level. To ask questions about a player — did they learn the route, did they loop, did they ever leave their corner — you need to follow one of them.
First, all eight routes at once. The line darkens as the match progresses, so you can read direction without playing anything. P03 covers the most ground (268 m). P07 travels almost as far (190 m) without ever leaving a two-metre-wide lane — it shuttles up and down the same corridor for the whole match. P01 and P02 manage 51 m and 35 m between them across three minutes.


Show the code
# Walls and the raised gantry, split so they can be shaded differently.
walls <- level %>% filter(kind != "elevated")
raised <- level %>% filter(kind == "elevated")

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = walls, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
            fill = "#2f2e2c", alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_rect(data = raised, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
            fill = "#6f6e6a", alpha = 0.55) +
  # Each player's route, darkening as the match goes on.
  geom_path(data = positions, aes(x, y, colour = t), linewidth = 0.7) +
  # One small panel per player, so you can compare routes side by side.
  facet_wrap(~player_id, nrow = 2) +
  scale_colour_gradient(low = "#cde2fb", high = "#104281",
                        name = "Time (s)", breaks = c(1, 90, 180)) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(0, 60), ylim = c(0, 40), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title    = "Eight routes through the same three minutes",
    subtitle = "Line darkens as the match progresses. Two players never leave the gantry.",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_tb() +
  theme(axis.text         = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major  = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor  = element_blank(),
        strip.text        = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ink[["primary"]]),
        legend.position   = "right",
        legend.key.height = unit(0.9, "lines"))









Now one player, animated, with the trail drawn behind them. Change focus_player to any ID from the panel above and re-run the chunk. The orange dots mark every second this player spent holding position, so you can see where they will stop before they get there.


Show the code
# Follow one player. Change this to any ID from P01 to P08.
focus_player <- "P06"

path <- positions %>% filter(player_id == focus_player) %>% arrange(t)

# For each second, every position so far. That's what makes the trail grow
# instead of jumping.
trail <- map_dfr(path$t, function(k) path %>% filter(t <= k) %>% mutate(f = k))

plot_ly(height = 560) %>%
  add_markers(
    data = path %>% filter(state == "Holding"), x = ~x, y = ~y,
    name = "Held position",
    marker = list(size = 7, color = pal[["orange"]], opacity = 0.7),
    text = ~paste0("holding · t=", t, "s"), hoverinfo = "text"
  ) %>%
  add_markers(
    data = path %>% slice(1), x = ~x, y = ~y, name = "Start",
    marker = list(symbol = "circle-open", size = 16, color = ink[["primary"]],
                  line = list(width = 2.5)),
    hoverinfo = "text", text = "start"
  ) %>%
  # The growing trail, then the player's current position on top.
  add_paths(
    data = trail, x = ~x, y = ~y, frame = ~f,
    line = list(color = pal[["blue"]], width = 2.5),
    opacity = 0.8, showlegend = FALSE, hoverinfo = "skip"
  ) %>%
  add_markers(
    data = path, x = ~x, y = ~y, frame = ~t,
    marker = list(size = 16, color = pal[["blue"]],
                  line = list(color = "#fcfcfb", width = 2.5)),
    showlegend = FALSE,
    text = ~paste0(focus_player, " · t=", t, "s · ", state), hoverinfo = "text"
  ) %>%
  layout(
    title  = list(text = paste0("<b>", focus_player, "'s route through the match</b>"),
                  x = 0, font = list(size = 14)),
    shapes = shapes,
    xaxis  = list(title = "x (m)", range = c(0, 60), constrain = "domain"),
    yaxis  = list(title = "y (m)", range = c(0, 40), scaleanchor = "x"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, title = list(text = "")),
    margin = list(t = 80)
  ) %>%
  animation_opts(frame = 70, transition = 0, redraw = FALSE) %>%
  animation_slider(currentvalue = list(prefix = "t = ", suffix = " s"))

None of this is difficult, and most of the length in Views 3 onwards is labelling and styling rather than analysis. All of it is repeatable: the same code runs unchanged on next week’s build, which is the real reason to write analysis as code rather than clicking through a spreadsheet.
The rest of these notes teach you the parts, in order, starting with the question that matters most: what are you actually trying to find out?

title: Lab 04 — Relationships in Your Data
text:
NoteGet the files




Data: tidebreak_sessions.csv, tidebreak_survey.csv. Save them in the data/ folder of your project.

title: Lab 04 — Relationships in Your Data
text:
Exercise 01 — What goes with score? [Do]
Use cor() to measure how strongly score is related to awareness, and to shots_fired.






NoteShow solution






cor(sessions$awareness, sessions$score)

[1] 0.5907852

cor(sessions$shots_fired, sessions$score)

[1] 0.05307857


cor() gives a number from −1 to +1. Near 0 means no straight-line relationship; the sign gives the direction.



Write 2 sentences: a designer wants to reward players who fire more shots, “because they are the ones scoring”. What do you tell them?

title: Lab 04 — Relationships in Your Data
text:
Exercise 02 — Pearson or Spearman? [Apply]
Do players who die more rate the game as harder? Draw difficulty against deaths, then compute both the Pearson and the Spearman correlation. Which would you report, and why?






NoteShow solution






ggplot(sessions, aes(x = deaths, y = difficulty)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0.15, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Deaths", y = "Difficulty rating (1-7)")







cor(sessions$deaths, sessions$difficulty)

[1] 0.5792729

cor(sessions$deaths, sessions$difficulty, method = "spearman")

[1] 0.5731608


The two agree closely, because the relationship is roughly straight with no wild values. Report Spearman anyway: difficulty is a 1–7 rating, so the gaps between its values are not known to be equal, and Spearman only uses their order. geom_jitter() nudges the points so that sessions with the same values do not hide each other.



Write 1 sentence: describe the relationship in words a designer would use, including how loose it is.

title: Lab 04 — Relationships in Your Data
text:
Exercise 03 — A correlation matrix [Apply]
Build a Spearman correlation matrix of deaths, wrong_turns, difficulty, enjoyment and session_minutes, rounded to 2 places. Then draw every pair with pairs(). Which pair goes together most strongly, and which measure goes with nothing?






NoteShow solution






m <- sessions |>
  select(deaths, wrong_turns, difficulty, enjoyment, session_minutes)

m |> cor(method = "spearman") |> round(2)

                deaths wrong_turns difficulty enjoyment session_minutes
deaths            1.00       -0.03       0.57     -0.20           -0.02
wrong_turns      -0.03        1.00      -0.09     -0.03            0.04
difficulty        0.57       -0.09       1.00     -0.33            0.15
enjoyment        -0.20       -0.03      -0.33      1.00            0.23
session_minutes  -0.02        0.04       0.15      0.23            1.00



pairs(m, pch = 19, cex = 0.4, col = adjustcolor("grey30", alpha.f = 0.4))








Ignore the diagonal of 1s and read one triangle. deaths and difficulty go together most strongly, 0.57. wrong_turns is close to 0 with every other measure. The pairs() panels agree: one rising band for deaths and difficulty, shapeless clouds for wrong turns.



Write 2 sentences: wrong turns differ hugely between the builds, yet correlate with nothing here. Why might that be, and what would you check next?

title: Lab 04 — Relationships in Your Data
text:
Exercise 04 — Telemetry against self-report [Apply]
Do players who got lost more rate the level as harder to navigate? Join the survey onto the sessions with left_join(), matching on session_id. Then find the Spearman correlation between wrong_turns and level_navigable, and each build’s mean of both.






NoteShow solution






joined <- sessions |>
  left_join(survey, by = "session_id")

cor(joined$wrong_turns, joined$level_navigable, method = "spearman")

[1] 0.05151128

joined |>
  group_by(build) |>
  summarise(mean_wrong_turns = mean(wrong_turns),
            mean_navigable   = mean(level_navigable))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  build mean_wrong_turns mean_navigable
  <chr>            <dbl>          <dbl>
1 A                 8.92           3.2 
2 B                 5.52           3.23


The correlation is 0.05: no relationship. Build A’s players made far more wrong turns but rated navigation almost exactly as Build B’s did, 3.2 against 3.23. The telemetry saw a navigation problem; the players did not report one.



Write 3 sentences: what does this mean for a team that only asks players whether the level was easy to navigate? What would observation add?

title: Lab 04 — Relationships in Your Data
text:
Exercise 05 — The trade-off [Apply]
Draw survivability against mobility as a scatterplot with a straight-line trend, and measure the relationship with cor().






NoteShow solution






ggplot(sessions, aes(x = mobility, y = survivability)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey40") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black") +
  labs(title = "Mobility against survivability",
       x = "Mobility rating", y = "Survivability rating")







cor(sessions$mobility, sessions$survivability)

[1] -0.6562375


geom_smooth(method = "lm") draws the straight line that best fits the points; se = FALSE leaves out the shaded band. The line and cor() describe the same relationship, one as a picture and one as a number.



Write 1 sentence: describe the relationship in words a balance designer would use.

title: Lab 04 — Relationships in Your Data
section: Exercise 06 — Faster players are more fragile? [Decide]
text:
Exercise 06 — Faster players are more fragile? [Decide]
The balance designer reads Exercise 05 and proposes a patch: “Faster players are more fragile, so when a Scout player gets faster, cut their health to match.” Redraw the scatterplot with each archetype in its own colour and its own trend line, compute the correlation within each archetype, and decide whether the patch follows from the data.






NoteShow solution






ggplot(sessions, aes(x = mobility, y = survivability, colour = archetype)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Mobility against survivability, by archetype",
       x = "Mobility rating", y = "Survivability rating", colour = "Archetype")







sessions |>
  group_by(archetype) |>
  summarise(r = cor(mobility, survivability))

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  archetype     r
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 Duelist   0.302
2 Engineer  0.512
3 Scout     0.465
4 Sentinel  0.598


One defensible answer: no, the patch reads the data backwards. Across all players the correlation is -0.66. Within every archetype it is positive, from 0.3 to 0.6. The downward trend is the gap between archetypes: Scouts are built fast and fragile, Sentinels slow and tough. Within any one archetype, better players are better at both. Archetype is the confounding variable: it drives both measures, and ignoring it reverses the direction of the relationship.
What makes it defensible. It checks the relationship inside the groups the design is made of before drawing a conclusion about individuals, and it says what the overall correlation does show: the archetypes are balanced against each other as intended.
What would make it indefensible. Applying the patch because the correlation is strong. A strong correlation across groups says nothing about what happens to one player within a group.



Write 3 sentences: name the confounder, say what it does to the conclusion, and say which section of the report (Results or Discussion) this belongs in.

title: Lab 05 — From Evidence to Report
text:
NoteGet the files




Data: tidebreak_sessions.csv, tidebreak_survey.csv. Save them in the data/ folder of your project.

title: Lab 05 — From Evidence to Report
section: Exercise 01 — Every survey item, both builds [Apply]
text:
Exercise 01 — Every survey item, both builds [Apply]
Reshape survey long, join each session’s build onto it, and find the proportion of players agreeing (4 or 5) with each item in each build. Which item moved most between the builds?






NoteShow solution






long <- survey |>
  pivot_longer(-session_id, names_to = "item", values_to = "rating")

agree_by_build <- long |>
  left_join(select(sessions, session_id, build), by = "session_id") |>
  group_by(item, build) |>
  summarise(agree = mean(rating >= 4), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = build, values_from = agree) |>
  mutate(change = B - A) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(change)))

agree_by_build

# A tibble: 8 × 4
  item                     A     B  change
  <chr>                <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
1 objective_clear     0.0833 0.383  0.3   
2 match_length        0.7    0.817  0.117 
3 death_understood    0.267  0.167 -0.1   
4 controls_responsive 0.717  0.8    0.0833
5 level_navigable     0.35   0.433  0.0833
6 would_play_again    0.5    0.517  0.0167
7 difficulty_fair     0.317  0.3   -0.0167
8 visual_style        0.933  0.933  0     


pivot_longer() makes item a column so one group_by() covers every item. pivot_wider() puts the two builds side by side so the change is one subtraction (Reshaping and Joining).



Write 2 sentences: objective_clear moved most. Which item would you have expected to move most, given what Build B changed, and did it?






NoteShow answer





level_navigable, since Build B added guidance to help players navigate. It moved from 35% agreeing to 43%, against objective_clear’s 8% to 38%. Build B cut wrong turns, but what players noticed was knowing where they were meant to go.

title: Lab 05 — From Evidence to Report
text:
Exercise 02 — “Without reducing enjoyment” [Decide]
The research question has two halves. Test the second: did Build B reduce enjoyment? Use enjoyment from sessions (1–7) and would_play_again from Exercise 01, and decide what the report may claim.






NoteShow solution






enjoy <- t.test(enjoyment ~ build, data = sessions)
enjoy$estimate

mean in group A mean in group B 
       3.933333        3.933333 

enjoy$conf.int

[1] -0.3483742  0.3483742
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

agree_by_build |> filter(item == "would_play_again")

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  item                 A     B change
  <chr>            <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
1 would_play_again   0.5 0.517 0.0167


One defensible answer: the report may claim no meaningful reduction. Mean enjoyment was 3.93 in Build A and 3.93 in Build B. The 95% confidence interval for the difference runs from -0.35 to 0.35 on a seven-point scale, so any true difference is small. Agreement with would_play_again was 50% and 52%. Two different measures agree.
What makes it defensible. It rests on an interval, not on “not significant”, and on two measures rather than one. It claims no meaningful reduction, which the evidence supports, rather than no effect, which no test can show.
What would make it indefensible. “The p-value is above 0.05, so Build B has no effect on enjoyment.” Or “Build B is just as enjoyable” from one measure with no interval.



Write 2 sentences: both measures were taken straight after one session. What would you need to know before claiming Build B is as enjoyable over a week of play?

title: Lab 05 — From Evidence to Report
text:
Exercise 03 — Code the comments [Apply]

title: Lab 05 — From Evidence to Report
text:
Exercise 04 — Do the sources agree? [Decide]
The telemetry says Build B players took far fewer wrong turns. Compare that with the comment codes from Exercise 03, by build and then by whether the player enjoyed the session (enjoyment >= 5). Decide what the report should say about navigation, and which evidence it should trust for what.






NoteShow solution






sessions |>
  group_by(build) |>
  summarise(mean_wrong_turns = mean(wrong_turns))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  build mean_wrong_turns
  <chr>            <dbl>
1 A                 8.92
2 B                 5.52

coded |> count(code, build)

# A tibble: 8 × 3
  code            build     n
  <chr>           <chr> <int>
1 Difficulty      A        19
2 Difficulty      B        16
3 Found the way   A        12
4 Found the way   B         9
5 General         A         6
6 General         B         4
7 Lost or unclear A        23
8 Lost or unclear B        31

coded |> count(code, enjoyed = enjoyment >= 5)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  code            enjoyed     n
  <chr>           <lgl>   <int>
1 Difficulty      FALSE      35
2 Found the way   TRUE       21
3 General         TRUE       10
4 Lost or unclear FALSE      54


The sources disagree. Build B players took fewer wrong turns, yet 31 Build B comments were coded lost or unclear, against 23 in Build A. Split by enjoyment instead of build, the codes separate cleanly: every lost or unclear comment came from a player who rated enjoyment below 5, and every found the way comment from one who rated it 5 or above.
One defensible answer. Trust the telemetry for what happened: Build B reduced wrong turns. Treat the comments as evidence about how the session felt: they track enjoyment, not build. Report both, in Results, and explain the gap in the Discussion. Recommend structured observation at the junctions in the next playtest, because nothing in this data shows whether players notice when they are lost.
What would make it indefensible. Leaving the comments out because they spoil the story, or reporting them as evidence that Build B made navigation worse.



Write 4 sentences, using What → Pattern → Meaning → Action, for the disagreement.

section: Exercise 06 — Discussion, Conclusion and Executive Summary [Decide]
text:
Exercise 06 — Discussion, Conclusion and Executive Summary [Decide]
Write the last three pieces of the Tidebreak report. Every number is inline R.

Discussion: whether the reduction in wrong turns matters to the player; the disagreement from Exercise 04; and at least three limitations specific to this playtest.
Conclusion: one finding in What → Pattern → Meaning → Action form that answers the research question.
Executive Summary: the question, the finding and the action, in three sentences. Write it last.







NoteShow solution






wt <- t.test(wrong_turns ~ build, data = sessions)
wt$estimate

mean in group A mean in group B 
       8.916667        5.516667 

wt$conf.int

[1] 2.480141 4.319859
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

sessions |> count(cohort, build)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  cohort  build     n
  <chr>   <chr> <int>
1 Novice  A        18
2 Novice  B        15
3 Regular A        26
4 Regular B        27
5 Veteran A        16
6 Veteran B        18


One defensible Discussion.

A reduction of 3.4 wrong turns per session is large enough for players to notice, and enjoyment did not fall. The comments disagree with the telemetry, but they track enjoyment rather than build, so we treat them as evidence about how sessions felt, not about navigation.
Limitations:

Each of the 30 players contributed 4 sessions, so the 120 sessions are not independent; the result holds when each player counts once.
Every measure was taken after one session. Nothing here shows whether the difference lasts.
Cohorts were not perfectly balanced between the builds; the cohort table is in the appendices so the reader can judge.
No observation was recorded, so we cannot say whether players noticed when they were lost.


One defensible Conclusion.

What. Wrong turns per session in 120 sessions, and enjoyment on a seven-point scale, compared between Build A and Build B.
Pattern. Build B players averaged 5.5 wrong turns against Build A’s 8.9, a reduction of between 2.5 and 4.3 per session at 95% confidence. Enjoyment was unchanged, with a mean of 3.93 in both builds.
Meaning. The guidance works, and costs nothing players noticed.
Action. Keep Build B’s guidance and carry it into the next build. Retest with an on-screen objective added, since objective clarity was the survey item that moved most, and add an observation sheet at the first two junctions.

One defensible Executive Summary.

Build B’s environmental guidance cut wrong turns by about 3.4 per session without reducing enjoyment. Players’ comments did not reflect the improvement, because they track how a session felt rather than where the player went. Keep the guidance, add an on-screen objective, and observe the junctions in the next playtest.

What makes it defensible. The limitations are specific to this data, and say what was checked. The Conclusion’s Action follows from its Meaning, and its Pattern gives a size and an interval. The Executive Summary stands on its own.
What would make it indefensible. “The sample was small” as the only limitation; a Conclusion whose Action (“improve the level”) no one could start on; or an Executive Summary that describes the method instead of the finding.



Write 3 sentences: which limitation would most change your Action if it turned out to matter, and how would you test it?

title: Lab 00 — Setting Up
text:
NoteGet the files




Data: tidebreak_sessions.csv, tidebreak_sessions_raw.csv, tidebreak_survey.csv, tidebreak_paired.csv, tidebreak_frame_times.csv.
Step 6 gets all of these by cloning or downloading the project. If you set up your own project instead, save them in its data/ folder.




Overview
Before any of the analysis labs will run, you need R, Quarto and an editor on your machine, and they need to be able to find each other.
This lab is not analysis. It is plumbing. Work through it in order and do not skip the checkpoints: each one tells you whether the previous step actually worked, which is much cheaper than discovering it in the middle of Lab 01.
Budget about forty minutes, most of which is waiting for downloads.


Choose your route
You can do every lab in this module with either of two editors. Pick one and follow it all the way through. You do not need both.









Route A — VS Code
Route B — RStudio




What it is
A general-purpose editor, plus R and Quarto extensions
An editor built specifically for R


Choose it if
You already use VS Code for other modules, or want one editor for everything
You are new to R, or want the least setup


Quarto
Installed separately (Step 2)
Comes bundled with RStudio


How you render
quarto render in the terminal, or the Render button
The Render button


Setup effort
More: the terminal must be able to find R and Quarto (Step 4)
Less: RStudio finds R by itself











Tool
Route A — VS Code
Route B — RStudio




R, the language that does the analysis
Yes
Yes


Quarto, turns a document containing R code into a web page
Yes, standalone install
Bundled, nothing to install


Editor
VS Code + two extensions
RStudio Desktop



The analysis labs work identically on both routes. The module’s live demos use VS Code, but nothing in a lab depends on it.
Most steps below have a VS Code tab and an RStudio tab. Click the tab for your route once: every other tab on the page switches with it.



Step 1 — Install R
Both routes. RStudio does not include R; it needs R installed first.
Windows. Download from cran.r-project.org → Download R for Windows → base → Download R x.x.x for Windows. Run the installer and accept the defaults.
macOS. Same site → Download R for macOS → the .pkg matching your chip (Apple silicon or Intel).
You need R 4.6.0 or later. If you have an older R from a previous module, install the new one anyway: packages are installed per R version, so you will install them again in Step 5.






WarningRoute A, Windows: the R installer does not add R to your PATH



This is deliberate on their part and inconvenient for VS Code users. Step 4 fixes it. Do not skip Step 4 just because the installer said it finished successfully. RStudio users can ignore this: RStudio finds R without PATH.




Step 2 — Install Quarto

VS CodeRStudio


Download the installer for your platform from quarto.org/docs/get-started and run it.
On Windows you can also use:
winget install --id Posit.Quarto






ImportantDo not rely on a copy inside RStudio



If you also have RStudio, it ships its own private copy of Quarto at a path like C:\Program Files\RStudio\resources\app\bin\quarto\bin. It is tied to your RStudio version and moves when RStudio updates. On the VS Code route, install Quarto properly as above.




Nothing to do. RStudio includes Quarto, and its Render button uses that copy. Skip to Step 3.






NoteOptional: a standalone Quarto as well





The bundled copy is only visible inside RStudio. If you also want to run quarto commands from a terminal, or get Quarto updates sooner than RStudio releases them, install it from quarto.org/docs/get-started too. The labs do not need this.








Step 3 — Install your editor

VS CodeRStudio


Download VS Code from code.visualstudio.com.
Then open the Extensions panel (Ctrl+Shift+X, or Cmd+Shift+X on macOS) and install:








Extension
Publisher
What it gives you




Quarto
Posit
Syntax highlighting for .qmd, a Render button, live preview


R
REditorSupport
R syntax highlighting and a console inside the editor





Download RStudio Desktop (the free version) from posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop and run the installer. Install R first (Step 1): RStudio looks for R when it starts.
Open RStudio. You should see four panes, one of them the Console, whose first lines report the R version, for example R version 4.6.0.






WarningWindows: RStudio picked up an old R





If the Console reports an R older than 4.6.0, you have more than one R installed. Go to Tools → Global Options → General → R version, click Change, choose the 4.6.x installation, then restart RStudio.








Step 4 — Make your terminal find R and Quarto

VS CodeRStudio


This is the step that causes almost every problem people report on this route. Two separate things go wrong.

Your PATH may not include R
Open a terminal in VS Code with Ctrl+` and run:
Rscript --version
If that reports a version, skip to the next heading. If it says not recognized, find your R installation and add it:
Get-ChildItem "C:\Program Files\R"
Take the folder name it reports — something like R-4.6.0 — and substitute it below:
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path", $env:Path + ";C:\Program Files\R\R-4.6.0\bin", "User")


Your terminal is holding a stale copy of PATH
A terminal keeps the environment it started with, and VS Code hands every new terminal a cached copy. So after installing anything, a brand new terminal panel will still not see it.
To refresh the terminal you are in right now:
$env:Path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path","Machine") + ";" + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path","User")
To fix it permanently, close VS Code completely — every window, not Reload Window — and reopen it.






NotemacOS and Linux



Both installers put R and Quarto on your PATH without help. If a command is not found, close the terminal and open a new one, and if that fails, restart VS Code.





Nothing to do. RStudio finds R and its own Quarto without using PATH. Skip to Checkpoint 1.






Checkpoint 1 — Are the tools visible?

VS CodeRStudio


Run all three in a VS Code terminal:
quarto --version
Rscript --version
code --version






NoteWhat you should see





Three version numbers. Quarto should be 1.4 or later and R 4.6.0 or later.
If any command is not recognized, go back to Step 4. Do not continue — nothing below will work.









WarningPowerShell: why R --version fails even when R works





R is a built-in PowerShell alias for Invoke-History, so R --version never reaches your R installation. You will see a confusing error mentioning “Cannot locate the history for command line”.
Use Rscript --version instead, or R.exe --version to bypass the alias. Rscript is the one that matters anyway — it is what Quarto calls.





Type this in the RStudio Console and press Enter:
R.version.string
Then check that RStudio knows about Quarto: open the File → New File menu.






NoteWhat you should see





The Console prints something like "R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24)": it must be 4.6.0 or later.
The New File menu lists Quarto Document…. If it does not, your RStudio is too old to include Quarto: install the current version from Step 3.








Step 5 — Install the R packages

VS CodeRStudio


In a VS Code terminal:
Rscript -e "install.packages(c('readr','dplyr','tidyr','ggplot2','knitr','rmarkdown'), repos='https://cloud.r-project.org')"






WarningPowerShell mangles quotes — use the right ones





Note the quoting above: double quotes outside, single quotes inside. PowerShell strips double quotes when passing arguments to a program, so the reverse arrangement arrives at R as install.packages(c(readr,dplyr,...), repos=https:/) and fails with unexpected '/'.





In the RStudio Console:
install.packages(c("readr", "dplyr", "tidyr", "ggplot2", "knitr", "rmarkdown"))
If RStudio asks you to choose a download mirror, pick any; 0-Cloud is fine.



Those six are all the labs need: readr reads the CSV files, dplyr and tidyr reshape and summarise data (from Lab 01), ggplot2 draws the report figures from Stage 3, and knitr and rmarkdown let Quarto run R. Installing them all now means no lab stops halfway for a download. Accept any prompt about a personal library.


Step 6 — Get the project and the data

VS CodeRStudio


git clone https://github.com/nmcguinness/L8-3DGD-Playtest-Analytics.git
cd L8-3DGD-Playtest-Analytics
code .
No Git? Use the green Code button on the repository page → Download ZIP, then unzip it and open the folder in VS Code with File → Open Folder.


With Git: File → New Project → Version Control → Git, paste https://github.com/nmcguinness/L8-3DGD-Playtest-Analytics.git as the repository URL, choose where to put it, and click Create Project.
No Git? Use the green Code button on the repository page → Download ZIP and unzip it. Then File → New Project → Existing Directory, browse to the unzipped folder, and click Create Project.






ImportantAlways work inside the project



An RStudio project sets the working directory to the project folder, which is why paths like data/tidebreak_sessions.csv work. Reopen it each time with File → Open Project (or the .Rproj file), not by opening a single .qmd on its own. The project name should show in the top-right corner of RStudio.





The data/ folder contains the CSVs every lab uses.



Checkpoint 2 — Render something
Create a new file called test.qmd in the project folder, beside the data/ folder, with exactly this content. (RStudio: File → New File → Quarto Document, choose Create Empty Document, paste, and save as test.qmd.)

Workflow
